AWS Certified Developer Associate (DVA-C02)

Learn the responsibility first, then choose the AWS feature that satisfies it. This guide connects theory → service decisions → payloads → practice. Service tiles open one reference containing its role, key features, comparison, example and AWS links.

Checked: 7 November 2026. The official DVA-C02 guide defines exam scope. Use the study roadmap to plan your next topics.

Architecture · Service cards · Cryptography · Practice · Part 2 · Part 3 review

1. Understand the application

Trace three connected flows: developer delivery → deployed application → user requests and background work. These are logical handoffs, not one packet path. Delivery configures resources and roles; the application uses its own runtime identity and constructs the response. Production evidence guides recovery and the next change. Select a box to study its responsibility, or trace a situation across lanes.

ARCHITECTURE BEFORE SERVICES One application. Find the flow that owns the problem.

Developers build, test, provision and release the application. Users invoke the deployed version; background workers finish asynchronous work. Identity, protection, resilience and observability apply across all three flows. Production evidence feeds recovery and the next revision.

Principles first; services replace the descriptions inside the same boxes.
Developer / delivery sequence Application requests / work Deployment / configuration Production feedback

Follow the arrowheads between boxes. Provisioning and release affect Application code; background work commits into State/cache. Feedback connects production evidence to Verify/recover and the next revision. Select a box to inspect its responsibility and handoffs.

Trace the handoff. Find the failed boundary.

A release changes what runs. A request uses it. An acknowledgement is separate from the business result.

Requirements

Define what correct behavior and a safe change mean before choosing a service.

Owns: Latency, allowed downtime/capacity loss, permissions, data lifetime and acceptable recovery.

Handoff: Acceptance criteria become code/tests, release gates and production health checks.

Boundary: Developer Associate focuses on implementing, testing and debugging applications; this map is a learning model, not a requirement to design an entire platform.

Example: Eight instances must keep serving during a batched rollout. “Some availability” is weaker than “full baseline capacity”.

Evidence: Write the baseline, temporary-capacity budget and health/rollback criteria before picking a deployment policy.

Elastic Beanstalk Lambda

Explore this boundary below ↓

Source / revision

Create an identifiable revision of the application, dependencies and infrastructure definition.

Owns: Source revision and the trigger that starts an existing delivery workflow.

Handoff: CodePipeline coordinates actions; a build action receives source and emits artifacts.

Boundary: The pipeline is the coordinator. It does not itself replace the build environment or runtime application.

Example: A source commit exists, but there is no release execution. Inspect the source connection/trigger and execution revision.

Evidence: Compare commit ID, source action result, trigger filters and pipeline execution history.

CodePipeline CodeBuild

Explore this boundary below ↓

Build / test

Turn a revision into a tested artifact that the chosen runtime can execute.

Owns: Buildspec commands, dependency packaging, unit/integration tests and immutable artifact identity.

Handoff: A versioned ZIP/image/template goes to deployment. The runtime later executes that artifact; CodeBuild is not the production server.

Boundary: Generated code/tests need review. Passing a build does not prove deployed IAM, integration behavior or production routing.

Example: The handler imports locally but fails after deployment. Check packaged files, runtime/architecture and dependency layout.

Evidence: Build/test reports, artifact contents/digest and runtime import errors should refer to the same revision.

CodeBuild CodePipeline SAM

Explore this boundary below ↓

Provision / configure

Create or update the resources and configuration that a running application depends on.

Owns: Declared resources, permissions, environment-specific values and resource lifecycle. Dynamic configuration has its own rollout.

Handoff: The runtime receives resources/roles/settings; release promotion selects the application revision and traffic route.

Boundary: CloudFormation can deploy application resources/code too. CodeDeploy adds specialized rollout behavior; they are complementary, not an absolute infrastructure/code split.

Example: The code is correct but a stack update changed the table/role configuration. Inspect stack events and resolved values.

Evidence: Change set, stack events/outputs, runtime configuration and deployment-role permissions locate a provisioning failure.

CloudFormation CDK SAM AppConfig Secrets Manager & Parameter Store

Explore this boundary below ↓

Release / promote

Make an approved revision receive traffic using a controlled deployment strategy.

Owns: Candidate version, deployment target, routing percentage, validation hooks and compatible rollback target.

Handoff: A Lambda alias, API stage or fleet route makes a particular artifact serve user requests.

Boundary: A published version is not automatically serving production. A canary routes a percentage; a parallel environment/fleet is a different isolation decision.

Example: The new package built successfully but users still see old behavior. Inspect the active alias/stage/fleet target.

Evidence: Compare artifact/version with the actual endpoint route, deployment record and request-correlated version logs.

CodeDeploy Elastic Beanstalk Lambda API Gateway

Explore this boundary below ↓

Verify / recover

Confirm that the deployed release works in its real environment, then recover or promote using evidence.

Owns: Post-deploy business/health checks, alarms, release validation and rollback execution.

Handoff: Production telemetry informs a rollback or the next code/configuration revision; it closes the application lifecycle loop.

Boundary: A successful deployment job is not evidence of business correctness. Check compatibility of database/configuration changes during rollback.

Example: The canary passes a basic health URL but order creation fails. Validate the real integration before expanding traffic.

Evidence: Deployment logs, critical-path tests, alarms, target health and the revision actually handling requests.

CodeDeploy CloudWatch, CloudTrail & tracing Application Load Balancer AppConfig

Explore this boundary below ↓

Client / caller

Make a request using the credential contract expected by the target.

Owns: Request payload, client-visible timeout, correlation/request ID and user/machine identity.

Handoff: The front door validates the caller; the backend later uses its own role to call AWS services.

Boundary: A Cognito JWT is for a supported token-verifying target. Direct AWS SDK access generally needs temporary AWS credentials and a signed request.

Example: A mobile user signs in but a direct S3 call fails. Decide whether the client needs identity-pool credentials or should call the application API.

Evidence: Inspect the actual target, token/credential type and issuer/audience/scope binding without logging secret values.

Cognito IAM, STS & Access Analyzer API Gateway

Explore this boundary below ↓

Trusted entry

Accept the request through a configured route and enforce the relevant entry controls.

Owns: API stage/integration, request transformation, token validation or IAM authorization and traffic controls.

Handoff: An authorized API invocation reaches the backend. Application code still checks business/record entitlement.

Boundary: REST and HTTP API features differ. An API key for a usage plan is not user authentication; an ALB route is not an IAM grant.

Example: A request never reaches the Lambda handler. Check authorizer/access logs, stage deployment and integration permissions.

Evidence: Distinguish entry 401/403, integration errors and backend errors before changing compute capacity.

API Gateway Application Load Balancer Cognito

Explore this boundary below ↓

Application code

Execute business logic against authorized data and downstream services.

Owns: Input/business validation, tenant entitlement, AWS SDK calls, error handling and request-scoped context.

Handoff: Read/write authoritative state, optionally publish background work, then construct the correct immediate response.

Boundary: The caller and execution role are different principals. A runtime role can access a table while the app user is still forbidden from a particular record.

Example: The API authenticates correctly but the backend receives AccessDenied from DynamoDB. Inspect the backend role and target policies.

Evidence: Correlate handler logs, role session, AWS action/resource and applicable policy denies; do not replace the caller token blindly.

Lambda EC2 ECS IAM, STS & Access Analyzer Fargate

Explore this boundary below ↓

State / cache

Persist authoritative data or reuse an appropriate cached copy.

Owns: Access keys/indexes or SQL endpoints, consistency, projection, cache scope and lifetime.

Handoff: Return data to application code, which constructs the client response. Background workers can update the same permitted state.

Boundary: A replica/index/cache has a distinct consistency contract. TTL cleanup is asynchronous; a cache key must separate users/tenants where required.

Example: A user sees stale or another tenant’s cached result. Check authoritative state, cache key and invalidation before adding capacity.

Evidence: Query/index or replica endpoint, projected fields, timestamps, cache hit/miss and tenant-scoped keys.

DynamoDB RDS ElastiCache S3 ECS

Explore this boundary below ↓

Response / outcome

Report what actually happened at the boundary the client is waiting for.

Owns: Response schema/status, truthful operation state and a way to correlate or poll asynchronous work.

Handoff: The caller receives success/failure or an accepted job ID. Telemetry records the request outcome.

Boundary: A 202/accepted response or successfully published event does not prove the background business operation committed.

Example: The API accepts an order, but fulfillment runs later. Return a job/order identifier and expose actual status separately.

Evidence: Match response semantics to the authoritative result record and trace/request ID.

API Gateway Lambda CloudWatch, CloudTrail & tracing

Explore this boundary below ↓

Route / fan out

Deliver a publication to matching or subscribed consumers when routing/fanout is needed.

Owns: Event schema, target selection, subscription/rule filters and publication/delivery errors.

Handoff: Targets can be queues, functions or workflows. An application can also send directly to SQS/Kinesis without this routing stage.

Boundary: Routing does not retain business-step progress. EventBridge bus types differ; select the exact feature contract rather than assuming identical guarantees.

Example: One publication must reach fulfillment and analytics independently. Fan out to separately authorized targets/queues.

Evidence: Inspect publish results, rule/filter matches, target permissions and delivery/DLQ evidence.

EventBridge & SNS SQS Step Functions

Explore this boundary below ↓

Buffer / retain

Decouple producer and consumer capacity with a queue, or retain stream records for consumption/replay.

Owns: Queue backlog/visibility/retention or stream partitioning/capacity and per-record ingestion outcomes.

Handoff: A worker receives a job or stream record; successful receipt is not completed processing.

Boundary: SQS and Kinesis are alternatives for different access/delivery needs. Inspect partial batch results and expect retries/duplicate side effects.

Example: PutRecords returns HTTP 200 with a failed entry. Retry that entry with backoff and investigate hot partition keys/capacity.

Evidence: FailedRecordCount and result positions for Kinesis; queue age/backlog, visibility and DLQ for SQS.

SQS Kinesis Data Streams

Explore this boundary below ↓

Worker / workflow

Perform background work, using a state machine only when multi-step coordination is required.

Owns: Task execution, workflow progress when used, bounded retries/catches and downstream failure handling.

Handoff: Persist a recoverable business result before acknowledging the source; carry the request/event ID through every step.

Boundary: A queue owns pending delivery; Step Functions owns workflow progress; Lambda/ECS executes code. CodePipeline belongs to software delivery.

Example: A payment call times out. Check the authoritative outcome before retrying, then recover using an idempotency key/result ledger.

Evidence: Worker logs, workflow execution history, receive count and downstream request/operation identifiers.

Step Functions Lambda ECS SQS Fargate

Explore this boundary below ↓

Commit / acknowledge

Keep duplicate delivery from turning into duplicate business effects and report completion accurately.

Owns: Atomic request claim, recorded result/status, recovery for abandoned work and acknowledgement ordering.

Handoff: Committed state becomes visible to permitted readers; only then acknowledge according to the source/integration contract.

Boundary: A conditional claim alone does not make an external payment exactly once. SQS deletion is not a database commit; Lambda event-source acknowledgements have their own contract.

Example: Two workers receive the same order. Use a conditional claim and persisted outcome; avoid a racing read-before-write check.

Evidence: Request ledger, condition failure, business result and acknowledgement timing show whether work is duplicated or lost.

DynamoDB SQS Step Functions

Explore this boundary below ↓

Identity / authorization

Apply separate identity and access decisions to delivery, users and machine workloads.

Owns: Developer/deployment roles, API token trust, backend/worker roles and application-level entitlements.

Handoff: Each trust boundary validates the correct principal/credential and permits only its intended action and data.

Boundary: A developer/deployment identity changes resources; the runtime uses its own configured role. Lambda assumes its execution role automatically. Explicit STS role switching is needed only for a separate session/trust requirement. Boundaries and SCPs restrict permissions; they grant none.

Example: The front door accepts a token but the app leaks another tenant’s record. Enforce record entitlement at the application/data access boundary.

Evidence: Token claims, route scopes, execution-role action/resource and tenant-filter decisions are distinct evidence.

IAM, STS & Access Analyzer Cognito API Gateway

Explore this boundary below ↓

Secrets / protection

Protect configuration, credentials and data without confusing protection with permission.

Owns: Secret rotation/retrieval, encryption keys, TLS/private paths and sensitive-data handling.

Handoff: Delivery configures references and policies; authorized runtime code retrieves values and uses protected resources.

Boundary: Encrypted data is not automatically authorized data. A security group permits a network path, not an IAM action or a business operation.

Example: The application keeps using a rotated password. Check runtime secret retrieval/cache behavior and the database integration.

Evidence: Secret version/rotation status, retrieval errors, KMS access and connection evidence; sanitize diagnostic logs.

Secrets Manager & Parameter Store KMS S3 Security groups, NACLs & VPC endpoints AppConfig

Explore this boundary below ↓

Resilience / performance

Keep failures bounded and match capacity to the measured bottleneck.

Owns: Timeout budgets, backoff/jitter, idempotency, concurrency, worker scaling and safe caching.

Handoff: Pressure/failure signals guide application/configuration changes and subsequent release validation.

Boundary: More capacity does not repair a policy deny or invalid request. Retries increase pressure unless paired with limits and idempotency.

Example: Queue depth grows while workers are busy. Compare backlog per worker and processing time; investigate downstream throttling before scaling blindly.

Evidence: Queue age, backlog per worker, duration/concurrency/throttles and downstream capacity reveal the limiting stage.

SQS EC2 Auto Scaling Lambda ElastiCache

Explore this boundary below ↓

Observability / feedback

Gather enough evidence to locate the first failed boundary and validate a change.

Owns: Structured logs, correlated requests/versions, metrics/alarms, traces and AWS API-change evidence.

Handoff: Production outcomes feed Verify/recover and the next code/configuration change; this closes the lifecycle loop.

Boundary: Metrics show trends, access logs show requests, traces locate stages and CloudTrail shows covered AWS API activity. Configure the evidence before an incident.

Example: Latency rises after release. Compare versions and a correlated trace before changing memory, replicas or queue capacity.

Evidence: Use the symptom’s metric to find the window, then request logs/spans, then relevant deployment/configuration events.

CloudWatch, CloudTrail & tracing Application Load Balancer CodeDeploy

Explore this boundary below ↓

2. Read the deciding constraint

Before choosing a service, name the principal, operation, state, failure mode and evidence. Then explain why the closest alternative fails.

Theory Ask in the scenario Typical boundary
Availability vs capacity Must some requests succeed, or must the full baseline keep serving? Rolling can preserve availability while reducing capacity.
Immutable vs mutable Are old instances changed, or does a new fleet/version coexist? A replacement fleet and an additional batch have different isolation/cost.
Authentication vs authorization Is this identity trusted, and may it perform this action on this data? JWT validation, AWS IAM access and record entitlement are separate checks.
State vs acceleration Is this the authoritative value, a replica or a cached copy? Replication lag and cache staleness affect correctness.
Delivery vs completion Was work accepted, processed, committed and acknowledged? A retry can repeat a side effect; use idempotency and recorded outcomes.
Signal vs evidence Do you need a trend, one request, a slow stage or an administrative change? Metrics, access logs, traces and CloudTrail answer different questions.

Use least overhead only after hard constraints are met. Prefer supported capabilities; measure the actual bottleneck before adding capacity or changing platforms.

Try the capacity boundary

Eight existing instances; batches of two. Compare a representative deployment phase after any extra instances pass health checks.

Rolling: six instances serve while two update. Rolling with an additional batch keeps eight serving by temporarily adding two. Immutable and traffic splitting launch a full replacement fleet.

Illustrative capacity, not an animation of every Beanstalk phase. Healthy, provisioned and traffic-receiving instances are different counts. Candidate health, quotas and deployment configuration still matter.

Client → front door → healthy execution → data → response

Front door, execution and capacity
CloudFront & global delivery Amazon API Gateway Application Load Balancer AWS Lambda Amazon EC2 EC2 Auto Scaling Amazon ECS AWS Fargate AWS AppSync
Runtime and front door

Which responsibility is required?

  • OS/host control
    EC2 (+ ASG capacity)EC2 EC2 Auto Scaling
  • Event-triggered function
    LambdaLambda
  • Manage container tasks/services
    ECS; choose EC2 or Fargate capacityECS Fargate EC2
  • Container process + shared persistent files

Configure the health-check contract separately from user routes. Network reachability and authorization are separate checks.

Implementation notes

Use a separate REST API stage for incompatible testing; stage variables supply environment configuration. Apply a canary when testing a percentage of live production traffic. Choose REST when its usage plans, managed cache or VTL body templates are required. Use scoped cache keys and verify REST vs HTTP support.

For compute, distinguish routing, provisioning, scaling and storage. Lambda layers package dependencies; memory affects conventional function CPU. An ASG adds EC2 instances; ALB sends requests to healthy targets. EFS keeps supported container tasks on shared persistent files, while task-local storage is disposable.

Desired is a target; current is observed capacity

Min/max bound the target. A scaling decision changes desired capacity; the ASG then launches or terminates instances to converge. This model counts ready instances as current and shows pending capacity separately; it omits weights, cooldowns and replacement surges.

Lab range: 0–50 instances for readability; this is not an AWS quota. Dots = ready, dashed + = pending.

Current 3, desired 5: two more instances are needed. Editing desired by +3 gives 8, subject to max 10; current remains 3 until launches complete.

Important correction. “Current 3, desired 5, +3 → desired 8” is a desired-target edit, not a universal step-policy rule. A step scaling adjustment can be based on current ready capacity and account for warming instances: 3 + 3 gives target 6, with two already pending. Repeated alarms need not add three again. Scale-in is blocked while instances warm in this simplified policy mode.

Exam trigger: min 1 allows the fleet to shrink to a single instance; multiple configured AZs alone do not guarantee two healthy targets. ASG maintains capacity; ALB routes requests, with its own health checks.

3.3 State & data access

Access pattern → key/index or SQL endpoint → consistency → cache/lifetime

Persistent state and acceleration
Amazon DynamoDB Amazon RDS Amazon ElastiCache
Data access and state

Which access pattern is the deciding clue?

  • Known partition/key lookup; flexible item fields
    DynamoDB; add GSI for another query keyDynamoDB
  • Relational read load
    RDS read replica; route reads explicitlyRDS
  • Relational failover
    RDS Multi-AZ; know instance vs clusterRDS
  • Repeated reusable result
    ElastiCache + expiry/invalidationElastiCache
  • Asynchronous cleanup of expired items
    DynamoDB TTLDynamoDB

A cache is not a SQL endpoint. An eventually consistent replica/index is not an immediate-read guarantee.

Implementation notes

For the game catalogue, GameName + Version identifies a version; GameName queries versions; Category + GameName on a GSI lists by category. Project the fields that the index must return. A GSI is eventually consistent. TTL removes expired items asynchronously; enforce application expiry even while an item still exists.

Route read-heavy SQL to a read replica when lag is acceptable. A traditional Multi-AZ standby supports failover; a Multi-AZ DB cluster can also serve reads. Cache-aside adds a separate lookup and invalidation path; it does not replace the relational endpoint.

One voucher, two writes — what if the second fails?

Transfer voucher V-42: delete Alice's ownership item, then put Bob's. A transaction makes both changes one atomic unit. A batch makes individual writes atomic, but allows partial success. This is a conceptual local model; the order of actual batch execution is not guaranteed.

  1. AliceOwns V-42
  2. Write boundaryTransaction: all-or-nothing
  3. BobNo voucher

Failure under a transaction: Alice keeps V-42; Bob receives nothing. Failure under a batch: Alice's delete may persist while Bob's put remains unprocessed.

# Conceptual SDK pseudocode; two distinct ownership items
TransactWriteItems([
  Delete(AliceVoucher, condition="owner = Alice"),
  Put(BobVoucher, condition="attribute_not_exists(PK)")
])
# BatchWriteItem supports Put/Delete, no conditions or Update.

ACID: Atomicity = all or nothing; Consistency = declared conditions/invariants remain valid when correctly modelled; Isolation = concurrent transactions behave serialisably for supported transactional operations; Durability = committed changes persist. A game purchase similarly couples balance debit with entitlement creation.

Both APIs are synchronous requests. Returning immediately vs waiting is independent of atomicity. A strongly consistent GetItem reads a recent committed item; it does not atomically coordinate multiple changes. Two independent strongly consistent reads are not one multi-item snapshot; use TransactGetItems for an atomic read set.

Delivery and duplicate control

Buffer, stream and retries

What is the delivery requirement?

  • Independent workers consume pending jobs
    SQS; acknowledge after successSQS
  • Replay stream records; ordered per shard
    Kinesis Data StreamsKinesis Data Streams
  • HTTP 200 with failed batch entries
    Inspect results; retry failed records onlyKinesis Data Streams

Backoff with jitter handles transient pressure. It does not repair invalid requests or authorize denied calls.

Event routing and application workflows
EventBridge & SNS AWS Step Functions
Route, buffer or coordinate?

What state does the service own?

  • Where does this publication go?
    EventBridge routing / SNS fanoutEventBridge & SNS
  • Which jobs are waiting for a worker?
    SQS backlogSQS
  • Which records can a consumer replay?
    Kinesis streamKinesis Data Streams
  • Which business step comes next?
    Step Functions state machineStep Functions

A producer can publish directly to a queue or stream. Use only the routing, buffering and coordination the application needs.

Implementation notes

On SQS, finish and record the outcome before deleting the message. Set visibility for processing time and extend it when appropriate; visibility does not remove the need for idempotency. Use an atomic conditional claim and recoverable result/status rather than read-before-write. For Kinesis batches, match per-entry results to input records and retry only failures with backoff and jitter.

Try backlog per worker

A queue of 1,000 jobs means different pressure with five workers versus fifty. Each worker here processes one message at a time.

1,000 / 10 = 100 messages per worker. A 60-second wait budget / 2-second processing time gives a target of 30 messages per worker.

A steady-state sizing estimate, not an exact latency guarantee or deployable scaling policy. Startup time, in-flight work, bursts and per-worker concurrency affect real capacity. An ECS policy uses running task capacity; an EC2 ASG uses InService instances. Configure a scale-from-zero signal.

Implementation notes

Separate the caller of your API from the role your code uses to call AWS. A role trust policy controls who can assume it; permission policies control subsequent actions. Boundaries and SCPs limit applicable permissions without granting them. Security groups and NACLs filter network traffic; encryption protects data. Neither grants application entitlement.

Trace the caller, token and permission

Start with the principal and target. User sign-in and backend AWS access can be parts of the same request.

Trust boundary: Public client → trusted identity issuer → API → application data

  1. User pool / external IdP1. Authenticate the app user
  2. Access JWT2. Bearer token for this API
  3. API authorizer3. Validate claims + required scope
  4. Application authorization4. Check tenant / record entitlement

Trust check: The API validates the trusted issuer, signature, expected client/audience binding, token type and expiry.

Permission check: The API must allow the requested scope/route; the application still checks the requested record or tenant.

Authorization: Bearer <access-token-JWT>
Cognito API Gateway IAM, STS & Access Analyzer

Trust boundary: Public client → identity federation → AWS IAM resource boundary

  1. User pool / supported IdP1. Authenticate; obtain identity token
  2. Cognito identity pool2. Validate identity + select trusted role
  3. Temporary AWS credentials3. Access key + secret + session token
  4. S3 / AWS API4. SigV4 request + IAM evaluation

Trust check: The identity pool accepts this provider/token; the role trust policy permits the intended federation path.

Permission check: Role/resource/key policies allow the exact operation and resource; applicable boundaries and organizational controls permit it.

AccessKeyId + SecretKey / SecretAccessKey + SessionToken + Expiration
Cognito IAM, STS & Access Analyzer S3

Trust boundary: Trusted AWS service → function execution role → target AWS resource

  1. Lambda service1. Run the function
  2. Execution-role trust2. Trust lambda.amazonaws.com
  3. Runtime credentials3. SDK credential provider obtains temporary credentials
  4. DynamoDB / S34. Signed request; evaluate role + resource policy

Trust check: The execution-role trust policy allows the Lambda service to assume it.

Permission check: The role and applicable resource/key policies allow the action; guardrails permit it. The app separately enforces its user’s entitlement.

SDK default credential chain → temporary role credentials → SigV4
Lambda IAM, STS & Access Analyzer DynamoDB
Change a check and follow the result

A simplified learning model. It does not implement IAM evaluation; resource policies, key policies, session policies, boundaries and organizational controls can change the result. Permission does not make an untrusted token valid.

Continue with the broader identity decision tree and JWT, OAuth, OIDC and SAML.

Store rotating credentials in Secrets Manager and static named configuration in Parameter Store as appropriate. For S3, distinguish resulting default encryption from a policy requiring explicit upload headers: AES256 means SSE-S3; aws:kms means SSE-KMS.

Cryptography — patterns, keys & AWS KMS

One question first: are you checking data, keeping it secret, or proving who signed it?

Scroll horizontally to compare the examples.

PatternThink of it as…Key directionExample calls · pseudocode
Hashing
Check content		A document's fingerprint; it does not contain the original document.No key; designed to be one-way.digest = SHA256(data)
No decrypt(digest).
Symmetric encryption
Keep data secret		A locked box with identical keys held by both sides.Same secret encrypts and decrypts.c = encrypt(data, shared_key)
data = decrypt(c, shared_key)
Asymmetric encryption
Send a secret		Share an open padlock; keep its unlocking key.Client: server's public key encrypts.
Server: private key decrypts.		c = encrypt(data, server_public)
data = decrypt(c, server_private)
SSH signature
Prove key possession		Your personal seal: others can check it without owning it.Client: private key signs.
Server: authorised public key verifies.		sig = sign(auth_data, client_private)
verify(auth_data, sig, client_public)

Exam traps: asymmetric encryption is not hashing; a plain hash does not authenticate its sender; Base64 only encodes data. SSH authenticates with a signature, then protects traffic with separate symmetric session keys.

AWS KMS — small secret vs large file

Analogy: KMS is a key vault. It can lock a small item for you, or protect the key you use to lock a large file yourself.

Small data · up to 4,096 bytes

KMS encrypts/decrypts the data with a symmetric KMS key that stays in KMS.

# Conceptual calls
blob = kms.Encrypt(secret, KeyId=K)
secret = kms.Decrypt(blob)
Large file · e.g. 111 GB

Client encrypts the file. KMS protects its data key.

# Conceptual envelope encryption
D, wrapped_D = kms.GenerateDataKey(K)
encrypted_file = AES_encrypt(file, D)
save(encrypted_file, wrapped_D, metadata)
clear_from_memory(D)

Another authorised client: D = kms.Decrypt(wrapped_D) → file = AES_decrypt(encrypted_file, D) → clear D.

Remember: D and wrapped_D are two forms of one data key. Keep plaintext D temporarily in client memory; store the encrypted key beside the ciphertext. KMS retains K, not both returned data-key copies. The second client still needs storage and KMS permissions.

Conceptual calls; see the references for SDK syntax and encryption metadata. Direct encryption limits · Envelope encryption · SSH authentication

KMS API comparison

Scroll the table horizontally on a narrow screen.

CallReturnsChoose when
EncryptCiphertextKMS directly encrypts small data
DecryptRecovered plaintextRecover data or a wrapped data key
GenerateDataKeyPlaintext + encrypted data keyClient needs to encrypt data now
GenerateDataKeyWithoutPlaintextEncrypted data key onlyDecrypt the data key when needed later

GenerateDataKeyWithPlaintext does not exist. “CMK” in older questions means a KMS key. Rotation does not automatically re-encrypt stored objects.

GenerateDataKey · WithoutPlaintext

Try it · KMS data-key request counter

Compare fresh materials per transaction with deliberately bounded reuse in one eligible cache.

Change the example

1,000 encryptions: fresh data keys ≈1,000 GenerateDataKey calls; batches of 100 eligible messages ≈10 calls. Real age, byte, context and cache-miss rules can refresh sooner.

Illustrative ceiling(transactions / reuse), not the exact Encryption SDK threshold algorithm. No cryptography, nonce generation, decryption calls or AWS requests run. Protect cached plaintext materials, retain unique required IV/nonces, and configure age/message/byte security limits. Local learning model; no AWS requests.

S3 encryption comparison

Scroll the table horizontally on a narrow screen.

ModeWho encrypts?Key controlKMS access?
SSE-S3S3S3 manages keys and rotationNo
SSE-KMS · AWS managed aws/s3S3AWS manages policy/rotation; customer cannot disable the keyYes
SSE-KMS · customer managedS3Customer controls key policy, disabling and supported rotation settingsYes: GenerateDataKey for upload; Decrypt for read/multipart
SSE-CS3Customer supplies the key over HTTPS; manages rotation; S3 does not retain itNo native KMS requirement
Client-side encryptionApplication before uploadApplication/library manages keys; S3 stores ciphertextIf the design uses KMS

Exam clue: control key policy, disabling or rotation → customer managed KMS key. Cross-account SSE-KMS sharing also needs a customer managed key and suitable S3/KMS permissions.

SSE-C rejects HTTP: the key must travel over HTTPS. To require HTTPS across S3 modes, use a bucket-policy Deny for aws:SecureTransport=false. SSE-C is blocked by default in new buckets and existing buckets in accounts without SSE-C objects (April 2026). See the S3 card for the transport-policy example.

Try it · Follow the S3 encryption key

Compare the direction of object data, a KMS key identifier and an actual customer-supplied key.

Change the example

SSE-S3: S3 manages keys. SSE-KMS: S3 uses KMS-protected data keys. SSE-C: client supplies actual key over HTTPS; S3 encrypts and does not retain it. SSE-C does not inherently use KMS.

All three encrypt on S3’s side. HTTPS is recommended throughout and mandatory for SSE-C. Bucket policies/key permissions and the current default SSE-C block still apply; this selector performs no encryption. Local learning model; no AWS requests.

SSE-KMS · SSE-C · Client-side encryption

Find the right evidence

Investigation Start with Then verify
How much traffic, latency or error rate? CloudWatch metrics Time window, dimensions, ALB vs target errors.
Which client/path/status/timing? ALB access logs Logging enabled, target/path and request correlation.
Where did request time go? Correlated application logs + distributed trace Downstream instrumentation and matching trace IDs.
Who changed an AWS setting? CloudTrail Relevant event type/coverage; application requests use their own access logs.
Why is a target unhealthy? Target health reason + configuration Security groups, NACLs, port, health path and success matcher.

See the AWS security/audit comparison for Config, Audit Manager, Artifact and findings services.

4. Practise the boundary

Choose a scenario and answer once. Explain the deciding constraint, reject the nearest alternative and name a change that would reverse your choice.

Original learning exercises: choose an answer to see the deciding clue and what would change it.

Practice Exam Follow-Up — Part 2

The related calculators and flow exercises live inside the existing service cards; this review tests the distinctions together.

One deciding detail at a time. Answer, check the boundary, then revisit the relevant service card.

LSI vs GSI — An existing Orders table needs a new OrderStatus partition-key lookup. Which index can be added?

LSI LSIs must be created with the table and share its partition key.

Best answer: GSI A GSI can be added later with another partition key; existing eligible items are backfilled.

Either index Creation timing and partition-key rules differ.

Think of it as: A new catalogue can use a new filing system; a local drawer keeps its existing key.

Revisit the service card
Shard vs stream capacity — Ten provisioned shards receive 5 MiB/s, but one gets 4 MiB/s. What explains write throttling?

The stream has no spare capacity The theoretical aggregate byte budget is 10 MiB/s, but it is not a shared pool.

Best answer: One shard exceeds its sustained write budget A shard is limited to 1 MiB/s and 1,000 records/s. Key skew can overload it despite idle shards.

Consumers deleted the shard Reads do not delete Kinesis records or shards.

Think of it as: Empty checkout lanes do not lend their capacity to one overloaded lane.

Revisit the service card
Kinesis exceptions — Which interpretation best distinguishes these errors?

LimitExceededException always means a hot shard It typically concerns service quotas/control-plane limits; inspect the operation.

Both mean the same thing Throughput pressure and service/API quota pressure need different investigation.

Best answer: ProvisionedThroughputExceededException indicates data-plane throughput pressure Investigate shard write/read limits for the failing operation; LimitExceededException typically concerns service or control-plane limits.

Think of it as: A busy checkout lane differs from the store’s limit on opening new lanes.

Revisit the service card
Eventual read arithmetic — A 12 KB item is read 16 times/s using eventual consistency. What steady read capacity does this require before headroom?

Best answer: 24 RCUs ceil(12/4) × 0.5 × 16 = 24 RCUs. Eventual reads consume half the strong-read units.

48 RCUs This is the corresponding strong-read rate, not eventual.

96 RCUs This is the corresponding transactional-read rate, not eventual.

Think of it as: Three cartons per item, half-price reads, sixteen orders per second.

Revisit the service card
Query vs Parallel Scan — A one-off export needs all items, no suitable key access exists, and spare read capacity is available. What can reduce elapsed scan time?

Query with only a FilterExpression Query still requires partition-key equality; a filter cannot supply it.

Best answer: Parallel Scan with paginated segment workers Concurrent logical segments can reduce time, while consuming capacity and requiring per-worker pagination.

ProjectionExpression makes the scan free Projection reduces returned fields, not Scan read capacity.

Think of it as: Several clerks can inspect separate filing-room sections, but each still reads the files.

Revisit the service card
Stateful vs stateless — HTTP reaches an ALB from Browser:54321, but the subnet outbound NACL allows only destination 80. What is missing?

Best answer: Response destination ephemeral port The response is ALB:80 → Browser:54321; the stateless NACL must allow that outbound destination.

A second inbound SG rule for source 80 SG tracking already permits the established response; the missing control is the NACL return path.

Change the browser source port to 80 Clients normally choose ephemeral source ports; the service destination is 80.

Think of it as: The return envelope is addressed to the caller’s temporary desk number.

Revisit the service card
Public frontend, private backend — Can an internet-facing ALB forward to an IP target in another VPC?

Only if the target has a public IP Publicly routable IPs cannot be registered as ALB IP targets.

Registration alone makes it reachable Registration creates no routing, security-group rules or return path.

Best answer: Yes, for a supported private IP with working connectivity Supported reachable private targets can be outside the VPC; routes, SGs, NACLs and health still apply.

Think of it as: A public reception desk can call a private office if a working connection exists.

Revisit the service card
Origins vs origin groups — An eligible GET must retry the same content from a backup after primary 503. What fits?

Multiple origins alone They let behaviours route different requests; they do not automatically define a failover pair.

Best answer: Origin group with configured failure conditions The behaviour targets a primary/secondary pair. GET can fail over on configured errors.

Merge both origin responses Origin groups retry; they do not combine responses.

Think of it as: Ask the backup shop for the same item, rather than combining two shopping baskets.

Revisit the service card
Dynamic delivery — /api/* returns dynamic JSON from an ALB. Does this alone require Lambda@Edge?

Best answer: No; ordinary CloudFront origin delivery can handle it Custom edge code is needed only when the request/response requires that custom processing.

Yes; every dynamic response requires edge code Dynamic content and custom processing are separate responsibilities.

Use Global Accelerator to cache JSON Global Accelerator is not a content cache.

Think of it as: Delivering a letter does not require rewriting it at every post office.

Revisit the service card
Shards vs replicas — Redis writes/storage need horizontal scaling across many well-distributed keys. What directly helps?

More replicas of the same shard Replicas copy that shard and support reads/failover; they do not add independent primary write partitions.

Enable cluster mode without adding shards The flag permits multi-shard topology, but does not itself add write capacity or replicas.

Best answer: Add shards and distribute the keyspace Each shard has a primary for its part of the keyspace; one hot key still maps to one shard.

Think of it as: Open another collection, rather than photocopying the same collection.

Revisit the service card
Queue encryption — A queue needs KMS encryption at rest with minimal application changes. Which fits?

Best answer: SSE-KMS plus appropriate IAM/KMS permissions SQS handles message encryption/decryption transparently for authorised clients.

Client-side encryption with no code changes Client-side encryption needs application encryption and key-handling logic.

Secrets Manager encrypts queue storage Secrets Manager stores secrets; SQS manages its own storage encryption.

Think of it as: The storage-room lock is managed by the queue, not installed by each visitor.

Revisit the service card
SSE-C and TLS — Who encrypts an SSE-C object, and how is the key supplied?

The client encrypts and never sends a key That describes client-side encryption, not SSE-C.

Best answer: S3 encrypts; client supplies the key over HTTPS SSE-C is server-side. S3 requires HTTPS and does not persist the supplied key.

S3 retrieves the customer key from Secrets Manager automatically That is not the SSE-C request model.

Think of it as: Lend the warehouse your key over a protected channel; it locks the box for you.

Revisit the service card
CodeDeploy lifecycle — Which sequence is correct for the core EC2 in-place lifecycle?

BeforeInstall → DownloadBundle → ApplicationStop ApplicationStop and DownloadBundle precede BeforeInstall.

DownloadBundle → ApplicationStop → Install ApplicationStop precedes the new bundle download and uses the prior successful revision.

Best answer: ApplicationStop → DownloadBundle → BeforeInstall → Install → AfterInstall → ApplicationStart → ValidateService This is the core order; DownloadBundle/Install are agent-reserved, and load-balanced deployments can add traffic events.

Think of it as: Stop → download → prepare → install → finish → start → test.

Revisit the service card
CodeCommit HTTPS — An IAM user needs a direct username/password for Git HTTPS to CodeCommit. What should they use?

Best answer: IAM-generated CodeCommit Git credentials These are service-specific Git credentials; a supported AWS credential helper is another approach.

AWS access key ID and secret as the raw Git login Those are not the direct Git HTTPS username/password.

GitHub PAT after git login A GitHub PAT authenticates GitHub, and Git has no standard git login command.

Think of it as: Use the badge issued for this repository host.

Revisit the service card
CloudFormation context — How should a template obtain its deployment Region without user input?

Declare AWS::Region as a String parameter It is a built-in pseudo parameter, not a user parameter declaration.

Best answer: !Ref AWS::Region CloudFormation resolves AWS-provided deployment context; CDK can leave it as an unresolved token during synthesis.

Hard-code it as a universal compile-time constant The deployment context can vary; hard-coding defeats reusable templates.

Think of it as: The office supplies its own address when processing your form.

Revisit the service card
API cache refresh — Which requests REST API entry invalidation when authorised and correctly configured?

?bypass_cache=1 This query parameter has no built-in API Gateway invalidation meaning.

Bypass-Cache: 1 This is not the required invalidation header.

Best answer: Cache-Control: max-age=0 With required execute-api:InvalidateCache permission and configuration, fetch a fresh backend response and update the entry.

Think of it as: An authorised check-again instruction replaces the cached order slip.

Revisit the service card
Detailed vs custom — An EC2 application must scale on memory utilisation. What is needed?

Only enable detailed monitoring Detailed monitoring increases native frequency; it does not add guest memory metrics.

Best answer: CloudWatch Agent or another custom memory publisher Publish guest memory, then configure the appropriate alarm/scaling policy.

ALB RequestCount without an ALB No ALB means no such metric; requests also do not directly measure memory.

Think of it as: A faster speedometer does not become a fuel gauge.

Revisit the service card
Identity vs resource policy — SNS must send to one SQS queue. Where is the queue access grant normally expressed?

Best answer: Queue policy: Principal sns.amazonaws.com, sqs:SendMessage, restricted source topic A queue resource policy grants the service principal access; add relevant KMS permissions for SSE-KMS.

An “SQS role” trust policy A queue policy is not a role trust policy, and SQS has no special identity type called an SQS role.

A permissions boundary by itself A boundary restricts permissions; it does not independently grant them.

Think of it as: Put the named delivery service on the room’s guest list.

Revisit the service card

Practice Exam Review — Part 3

Practise cache ownership, permission direction, index capacity and delivery boundaries. The examples remain in their service cards.

One deciding detail at a time. Answer, check the boundary, then revisit the relevant service card.

DAX vs general cache — A product catalogue repeats eventual DynamoDB reads and wants minimal custom cache population/invalidation code. Which fits best?

Best answer: DAX with a compatible client/endpoint DAX manages the eligible item/query cache path. Results can be shared by clients using the same relevant keys/queries.

Redis because it cannot cache DynamoDB otherwise Redis absolutely can cache DynamoDB; it needs application-managed cache logic, so the stated reason is false.

CloudFront as a direct DynamoDB SDK cache CloudFront caches HTTP representations, not native DynamoDB SDK operations.

Think of it as: Use a DynamoDB-aware librarian rather than organising every cache shelf yourself.

Revisit the service card
Strong reads and DAX — A DAX client requests ConsistentRead=true on a supported table read. What should you expect?

A strong read served from the DAX cache DAX cache hits are eventually consistent; this would misstate the guarantee.

Best answer: DAX forwards the read to DynamoDB without caching that strong result The strong consistency requirement is met by DynamoDB, not by a DAX cache hit.

DAX converts it to an eventual GSI read DAX does not change the requirement into a GSI read; GSIs cannot serve strong reads.

Think of it as: Go to the original signed ledger when the latest committed entry is required.

Revisit the service card
Which permission direction? — API Gateway accepts a caller but fails before a Lambda function executes. Adding DynamoDB access to the Lambda role did not help. What should you inspect?

Only the Lambda execution role That role controls outgoing AWS calls after the function runs.

The client’s Redis session TTL It does not grant the API Gateway integration permission to invoke Lambda.

Best answer: The selected integration target and API Gateway invocation permission Check the function/alias resource policy or correctly configured invocation role. Missing permission can cause HTTP 500.

Think of it as: The receptionist needs permission to call the office before the office can open its filing cabinet.

Revisit the service card
STS vs authorisation — A client assumes an IAM role, then calls an AWS_IAM-protected API. What authorises the incoming request?

API Gateway treats STS as a built-in authoriser STS supplies credentials; it is not a standalone API Gateway authoriser.

Best answer: IAM evaluation of a properly signed request using the temporary credentials The client uses the STS-issued key/session credentials to sign, normally with SigV4, and needs execute-api:Invoke.

Lambda’s execution role authenticates the client That role controls the function’s downstream AWS permissions, not incoming API caller authorisation.

Think of it as: STS issues the badge; the API checks the badge and its permitted access.

Revisit the service card
Stage variable vs grant — dev defines lambdaFunction=my-api-dev and prod defines my-api-prod. What does the variable itself provide?

Best answer: Configuration selecting the integration target Stages hold key/value settings; the integration can interpolate a function/alias, which still needs invocation permission.

lambda:InvokeFunction permission on both functions A configuration value is not a policy grant.

A new Lambda execution role for every call Variables do not provision execution roles or isolate application state automatically.

Think of it as: Changing the office number in a directory does not give you an access badge.

Revisit the service card
Projection vs filtering — A Users Scan should return Name/Email only, and only active users. Which description is correct?

Projection filters rows and filter selects columns Those responsibilities are reversed.

Projection/filter reduce read capacity for the same evaluated items They reduce output, not the underlying read capacity for evaluating those items.

Best answer: Projection chooses attributes; filter removes non-matching items after reading Use expression aliases where needed. A suitable key/index can avoid a full Scan; output filters alone do not.

Think of it as: Choose spreadsheet columns separately from which rows remain visible.

Revisit the service card
FIFO group boundary — Two users’ purchases need per-user order, with different users processing concurrently. What should the producer set?

Best answer: MessageGroupId=user_id Same-group order is preserved; different groups can progress concurrently.

One shared group for every user This serialises all users into one ordering boundary instead of permitting cross-user group parallelism.

MessageOrderId=user_id MessageOrderId is not an SQS SendMessage parameter.

Think of it as: One checkout lane per ordering group, rather than one lane for the whole store.

Revisit the service card
Deduplication does not delete — A FIFO message was processed and deleted. The producer retries the same logical MessageDeduplicationId two minutes after the first send. What occurs?

SQS deletes any newer queued message Deduplication suppresses the duplicate send; it is not a delete request.

Best answer: The retry can be acknowledged without a new deliverable message Deduplication history persists for the five-minute window even after the original message is deleted.

A new message must be delivered because the first was deleted Deletion does not automatically remove the send-deduplication history.

Think of it as: A used receipt number remains recognised after the original order is collected.

Revisit the service card
Declared vs packaged dependency — A Lambda ZIP contains index.js and package.json listing pg, but no installed pg code or dependency layer. What is missing?

Lambda must be told to run npm install at each cold start ZIP deployment does not automatically install npm dependencies; build/install before deployment.

A bigger memory setting More CPU/memory does not supply the missing module files.

Best answer: Installed/bundled dependencies in the artifact or a configured layer Run npm ci/install at build time; include required runtime code and correct archive paths.

Think of it as: A shopping list is not the ingredients in the pantry.

Revisit the service card
Index write back-pressure — One hundred new items/s each require a 1.5 KB GSI entry. The GSI has 150 WCUs; table capacity is ample. What is the concern?

Best answer: The GSI needs 200 WCUs before headroom and can back-pressure base writes ceil(1.5/1) × 100 = 200 index WCUs. Its insufficient write budget can throttle associated table writes.

The GSI can borrow spare base-table WCUs automatically Provisioned GSI capacity is separate, unlike LSI capacity.

Only GSI queries can throttle; base writes are unaffected An under-provisioned GSI write path can throttle base-table writes.

Think of it as: A fast factory can still back up when its required indexing desk cannot keep pace.

Revisit the service card
Index read budget — A GSI Query retrieves one projected 12 KB entry per request at 16 requests/s. What eventual read budget applies before headroom?

48 base-table RCUs That is strong-read arithmetic; GSI queries use their own eventual-read capacity.

Best answer: 24 GSI RCUs ceil(12/4) × 0.5 × 16 = 24 RCUs on the index. This example has one returned/evaluated entry per Query.

No read cost because the table was already indexed A GSI has its own reads, storage and affected-write costs.

Think of it as: Pay the separate catalogue’s read desk at the eventual-read rate.

Revisit the service card
Stable-IP cutover — A replacement must preserve the public IPv4 of an EC2-hosted service. Which approach fits, with the right caveat?

Route 53 automatically preserves the EC2 public IP DNS answers can point to addresses; failover does not make a new instance inherit an old address.

Stopping the old server guarantees zero downtime A period without a ready serving instance is disruptive.

Best answer: Prepare/test the replacement, then reassociate the EIP in its Region The IP stays stable, but reassociation and connection recovery can briefly interrupt traffic.

Think of it as: Keep the phone number while transferring it to a prepared office; calls can still drop.

Revisit the service card
Query string cache key — The origin returns the requested review language, but CloudFront serves English for lang=jp after caching lang=en. What should change?

Best answer: Include lang in the cache key and ensure it reaches the origin Different representations need distinct keys; origin-request forwarding alone does not distinguish cached objects.

Only reduce TTL A shorter TTL does not make a key that ignores language correct.

Replace the query parameter with an unrelated header automatically Headers and query parameters are different inputs; a matching cache/origin design is still required.

Think of it as: Translated folders need language labels, not just a faster replacement schedule.

Revisit the service card
Historical CodeStar clue — An older question describes a unified AWS development project dashboard. What is the accurate modern reading?

CodeStar is the recommended new dashboard today The original CodeStar project capability retired in July 2024.

Best answer: The old clue may mean CodeStar; use current CI/CD tools for current designs CodeBuild builds/tests, CodeDeploy deploys and CodePipeline orchestrates. CodeConnections is a separate capability.

CodeConnections retired with the CodeStar dashboard The old CodeStar Connections name does not imply the separate connection service was retired.

Think of it as: Recognise the old control-room name without trying to open a retired control room.

Revisit the service card
KCL shard leases — One KCL application has 10 shards and 20 one-worker EC2 instances. What is the settled shard-level allocation limit?

Twenty workers each get half a shard lease The basic lease-processing model assigns a shard to one active worker within an application.

Only one worker can read the entire stream One worker can own multiple shards, but multiple workers can own different shards.

Best answer: At most 10 workers do shard-level processing; the others have no shard lease More workers do not create more shards. Independent consumer applications have separate ownership sets.

Think of it as: Twenty clerks cannot create twenty checkout lanes in a ten-lane store.

Revisit the service card
Data-key request reduction — An illustrative single-client model encrypts 1,000 matching-context messages, with 100 uses per cached data key and no earlier age/byte expiry. About how many fresh data-key calls occur?

Best answer: 10 ceil(1000/100) = 10 in this simple model. Actual SDK thresholds, misses and contexts can refresh sooner.

1,000 regardless of eligible caching Fresh-per-message would need approximately 1,000; eligible bounded caching is intended to reduce those requests.

Zero because KMS stores the client cache A fresh key still needs initial materials; the application/SDK cache is not automatically stored by KMS.

Think of it as: A bounded batch reuses a protected work key, then requests a fresh one.

Revisit the service card
Data-key caching safety — Eligible data-key caching is enabled. Which assumption remains unsafe?

Age, message and byte thresholds can limit reuse Those are useful security boundaries, along with supported algorithm/context handling.

Best answer: The same key means an IV/nonce may be reused for every encryption Key reuse does not permit nonce/IV reuse. Follow the SDK’s cryptographic construction and protect cached materials.

S3 Bucket Keys are specific to S3 SSE-KMS Correct: they are not an arbitrary application-transaction data-key cache.

Think of it as: Reusing a protected work key is not reusing the same per-message seal.

Revisit the service card
TTL does not refresh — Popular profiles tolerate up to 60 seconds of staleness and cache space is limited. What fits, and what happens at expiry?

Write every profile into cache; expiry proactively queries the DB That caches never-read profiles, and ordinary TTL expiry does not automatically fetch the source.

Lazy loading without TTL guarantees the 60-second bound Without expiry/invalidation, a cache-aside entry can remain stale much longer.

Best answer: Lazy loading + TTL; the next read after expiry fetches/populates Only requested items are cached, with an expiry boundary; real concurrency/failures still need consideration.

Think of it as: The use-by label invalidates the shelf copy; a customer’s next request restocks it.

Revisit the service card
Update vs delete cache — After committing a new product price, the app should avoid maintaining the new cached representation. Which pattern fits?

Best answer: Delete the cache entry after the DB write; next read repopulates Write-invalidate differs from write-through, which sets the updated cached representation. Handle deletion failure and read/write races.

Call TTL and assume it updates the cached price immediately TTL expiration does not write a new cached value or guarantee an immediate refresh.

Use two ordinary writes as an atomic DB/cache transaction Separate DB/cache calls are not automatically atomic; strict freshness needs stronger controls.

Think of it as: Remove the old price card; the next reader fetches the new one.

Revisit the service card
Gateway route vs interface ENI — Private EC2 needs ordinary same-VPC DynamoDB access without NAT and with minimal endpoint cost. Which statement fits?

DynamoDB supports only interface endpoints It supports gateway and interface endpoints.

Best answer: A gateway endpoint uses a prefix-list route; a DynamoDB interface endpoint is also supported for other needs Gateway access needs the route-table association, no endpoint ENI/SG, and no additional endpoint charge.

A gateway endpoint always resolves to a new private ENI IP That describes the interface-endpoint mechanism, not a gateway route.

Think of it as: Change a route sign for a gateway; build a private-IP entrance for an interface endpoint.

Revisit the service card
Role detachment and bucket access — An EC2 role was detached and its old credentials expired. Reads still work through a bucket policy explicitly allowing anonymous GetObject, with BPA permitting it. Why?

S3 gives a five-minute read grace period There is no special five-minute read grace period.

The expired role credentials still authorise signed requests forever Expired credentials do not provide a valid authenticated role identity.

Best answer: The anonymous request has a separate applicable resource-policy grant The scenario explicitly permits public reads. Named-principal bucket grants would still need matching valid credentials; other controls can deny.

Think of it as: Closing the badge dispenser does not close a separately permitted public doorway.

Revisit the service card
CLI output pages — A 250-object listing uses --max-items 100. How does the caller obtain the next output page?

Best answer: Pass the prior CLI NextToken unchanged as --starting-token This yields the next output page: 100, 100, then 50 objects in the fixed dataset. --page-size controls underlying calls.

Pass --next-token as the generic CLI paginator input That is not the corresponding CLI input; command-specific service tokens are a separate concept.

Set --page-size 100 and expect it to stop total output at 100 Page size controls each service call, not the complete automatically paginated output.

Think of it as: The clerk’s claim ticket resumes your output pile; box size controls warehouse deliveries.

Revisit the service card
Searchable trace data — Traces must be searchable by tenant, with a nested debugging payload retained for inspection. Where should each go?

Tenant in metadata; nested object in an annotation Metadata is not indexed, and annotations are scalar indexed values.

Best answer: Tenant annotation; nested object in metadata Use an annotation filter to find traces, then inspect non-indexed metadata. Segments describe service work, not infrastructure stacks.

Put both in the sampling rate Sampling controls whether requests are traced, not their indexed business labels.

Think of it as: Use an indexed parcel label to find the package; read the detailed note inside it.

Revisit the service card
Worker scheduling — A Beanstalk app must enqueue hourly video jobs for its worker HTTP endpoint. What is the native scheduling path?

A web-tier package.json cron field creates scheduled SQS messages That is not the Beanstalk native scheduled-worker mechanism.

.ebextensions is the recurring-job schedule file It configures/provisions the environment; it is not cron.yaml.

Best answer: Worker-tier cron.yaml → scheduler → SQS → daemon → application POST The scheduler enqueues; the daemon delivers work to the local application endpoint. Jobs still need retry/idempotency handling.

Think of it as: The timetable creates a ticket, the queue holds it, and the worker delivers it to the back office.

Revisit the service card
Actual key vs key identifier — The customer sends an actual encryption key to S3 over HTTPS; S3 encrypts and does not persist that key. Which mode is this?

Best answer: SSE-C; it does not inherently require KMS S3 performs the cryptography with the supplied key. SSE-KMS instead uses KMS-protected data keys and normally a key identifier, not customer plaintext key material.

SSE-KMS because all customer keys require KMS import Importing key material into KMS is separate from supplying an SSE-C key.

Client-side encryption because the customer owns the key Client-side means encryption happens before upload; in this scenario S3 encrypts.

Think of it as: Lend the warehouse your key to lock the box; you have not delivered an already encrypted box.

AWS Elastic Beanstalk

Deploy an application; let Beanstalk coordinate its infrastructure.

  • Standard environments manage EC2, load balancing, scaling, deployment and health.
  • Use .ebextensions/<name>.config (YAML/JSON) for environment options, instance customization and extra CloudFormation resources.
  • Environment-created resources normally share its lifecycle; keep durable RDS outside it. A disposable session cache can be recreated.

Decision boundary. Rolling can reduce serving capacity and leave mixed versions after failure. Immutable/traffic splitting replace the fleet and lose accumulated CPU burst credits. Blue/green uses separate environments and a CNAME swap.

What can .ebextensions define?

These are configuration files, not an extension marketplace. Put YAML/JSON .config files in your source bundle's .ebextensions/ folder. They configure Beanstalk Standard environments.

Scroll the table horizontally to compare columns.
KeyWhat it definesExample
option_settingsBeanstalk options in namespacesEnvironment variables, instance/scaling settings, health checks, deployment policy
packagesInstall instance softwarejq, OS libraries; documented handlers include yum, rpm, rubygems and python, subject to platform support
sourcesDownload and unpack archivesExtract a helper bundle into an instance directory
filesWrite/download files with ownership and permissionsCreate an application configuration file
users / groupsLocal OS accounts and groupsA system user for a helper process
commandsRoot commands before the application archive is extractedPrepare OS directories/tools
container_commandsCommands in application staging, before deploymentCompile assets; leader_only selects one instance for a deployment task
servicesConfigure supported OS servicesEnable/start a daemon; this does not provision an AWS managed service
ResourcesAny CloudFormation-supported resource typeElastiCache, SQS, SNS, alarms, IAM roles or RDS; creation needs appropriate permissions

Install ≠ provision. packages installs software on the EC2 instances. Resources → AWS::ElastiCache::CacheCluster creates a separate managed cache in the environment's CloudFormation stack.

Lifecycle. A stack-owned cache normally disappears when the environment is terminated. CloudFormation DeletionPolicy: Retain or supported snapshot policies can change cleanup. Referencing an external cache/database does not transfer ownership; resources created separately by a script are not automatically tracked by the stack. Keep durable/shared data in a separate stack.

Modern Linux. Use application manifests such as requirements.txt / package.json for runtime dependencies, and platform hooks (.platform/hooks/prebuild, predeploy, postdeploy) for custom scripts. Match packages and service management to the OS/runtime. container_commands refers to app staging; it does not require Docker.

StrategyExtra instancesServing capacity / deciding clue
All at onceNoneMay drop to zero; quickest rollout
RollingNoneReduced by the batch being updated
Rolling + additional batchOne temporary batchMaintains baseline capacity
ImmutableReplacement fleetKeep old fleet intact while validating new
Traffic splittingReplacement fleetCanary percentage; requires ALB
Managed environment, underlying CloudFormation

Elastic Beanstalk uses CloudFormation to launch environment resources, then manages deployments, health and scaling. An .ebextensions Resources definition extends that environment stack; disposal/retention rules still matter.

Inspect Beanstalk events and underlying stack events for provisioning failures. Avoid uncoordinated manual changes to managed resources. A failed immutable rollout and a failed in-place rolling rollout have different rollback/isolation boundaries.

Common trap. Environment-managed infrastructure is not proof that every custom script-created external resource is tracked or safely retained.

Worker tier: scheduled jobs use cron.yaml and SQS

Think of it as: The timetable creates a work ticket; SQS holds tickets until a worker calls the back-office endpoint.

  1. 1 · cron.yaml
  2. 2 · Leader scheduler
  3. 3 · SQS
  4. 4 · Worker daemon
  5. 5 · POST /process-videos

Web server environments handle user HTTP requests; worker environments process background jobs from SQS. A leader scheduler uses cron.yaml in the application source bundle to enqueue recurring work. The worker daemon polls SQS and POSTs to the application’s local HTTP endpoint; a successful response lets it delete the message.

.ebextensions/*.config customises environment resources/configuration. cron.yaml is the native recurring worker-task mechanism. OS cron can be installed/configured separately, but is not the same scheduling path. Jobs must tolerate retries and duplicate delivery.

Scroll the table horizontally on a narrow screen.

PurposeUseBoundary
User-facing HTTPWeb server environmentHandles requests through the web tier
Queued background jobWorker environment + SQSDaemon forwards message body to local app endpoint
Recurring worker jobcron.yamlSchedule + endpoint path; scheduler enqueues
Environment provisioning/settings.ebextensions/*.configDifferent file and responsibility
 
# cron.yaml at source-bundle root; worker tier
version: 1
cron:
  - name: "process-videos"
    url: "/process-videos"
    schedule: "0 * * * *"
# Scheduler → SQS → daemon → POST /process-videos (hourly).

Exam trigger. Native scheduled Beanstalk background task → worker tier + cron.yaml, not a web-tier cron file.

Common trap. A schedule enqueues work; it does not guarantee exact execution time or exactly-once side effects.

.ebextensions/01-environment.config · illustrative Linux excerpt 
option_settings:
  aws:elasticbeanstalk:command:
    DeploymentPolicy: RollingWithAdditionalBatch
    BatchSizeType: Fixed
    BatchSize: 2

# Install a tool on the environment's EC2 instances.
packages:
  yum:
    jq: []

# Provision a managed cache in the environment stack.
Resources:
  SessionCache:
    Type: AWS::ElastiCache::CacheCluster
    Properties:
      Engine: memcached
      CacheNodeType: cache.t3.micro
      NumCacheNodes: 1
      CacheSubnetGroupName: example-cache-subnets
      VpcSecurityGroupIds:
        - sg-0123456789abcdef0

Replace the cache subnet group/security group placeholders with compatible existing VPC resources and allow application access to the cache. This excerpt omits network setup; it has no retention policy, so the cache follows environment deletion. On a failed rolling deployment, replacement instances use the last successful app version; redeploy to restore consistency.

Amazon EC2

A virtual machine with OS and instance-level control.

  • Linux user-data shell scripts run as root, normally on the first launch boot only. Configure cloud-init explicitly for later boots.
  • Stop an EBS-backed instance before changing its user-data attribute; changing it does not itself rerun the script.
  • T-family instances spend CPU credits on bursts; sustained CPU demand needs an appropriate family or credit configuration.

Decision boundary. Hardware isolation alone points to Dedicated Instances; physical host placement or socket/core licensing points to Dedicated Hosts.

Free Tier: which account offer applies?

Checked 7 November 2026. The “t2.micro free for your first 12 months” wording describes the legacy offer used in older learning material.

Scroll the table horizontally to compare columns.
Limit / ruleLegacy: account created before 15 July 2025Current: account created on/after 15 July 2025
Compute allowance750 eligible instance-hours/month, subject to the applicable OS offer; not 750 hours per instanceUSD $100 at signup + up to $100 earned credits, shared across eligible AWS services; no blanket 750-hour EC2 allowance
DurationFirst 12 months after account creation, not after launching the instanceFree plan ends after 6 months or credit exhaustion, whichever is first. On a Paid plan, remaining credits apply until expiry, no later than 12 months after signup.
Eligible instance typest2.micro / t3.micro, subject to offer/Region and eligible AMICurrently marked eligible: t3.micro, t3.small, t4g.micro, t4g.small, c7i-flex.large, m7i-flex.large; use a compatible eligible AMI
EBS (separate from compute hours)30 GB storage, 2 million eligible I/Os and 1 GB snapshot storage under the legacy EBS offerEligible EBS usage consumes the shared credits; selecting an eligible instance does not make its disks unlimited
Public IPv4750 in-use address-hours/month during the 12-month offerEligible address charges consume credits; check your account's offer rather than assuming legacy IP hours
Beyond the allowanceStandard charges for excess usage or after the 12-month periodFree plan closes when it expires unless upgraded. Paid plan bills usage beyond credits or outside credit eligibility.

Legacy example. One eligible Linux instance × 24 h × 31 days = 744 instance-hours. Two under the same offer = 1,488 hours. Add usage across instances and Regions within that offer; the allowance is not per server or Region.

Free cost ≠ billing granularity. “0 seconds” is not EC2's general minimum billing duration. Eligible per-second billing has a 60-second minimum; an applicable allowance or credit can cover the charge. Check Billing → Free Tier / Credits for your actual eligibility, balance and expiry.

Try it · Replacement deployment cutover

Compare the gap with no ready server, stable-IP reassociation, and independent-server redundancy.

Change the example

Prepare-and-move EIP keeps one public IPv4 address but may briefly interrupt traffic. DNS redundancy uses different endpoints and has detection/caching considerations.

Qualitative comparison only; no universal downtime seconds are claimed. EIPs are regional public IPv4 addresses. A redundant authoritative DNS design differs from simply changing an A record. Local learning model; no AWS requests.

Regional vs Zonal Reserved Instances

Scroll the table horizontally on a narrow screen.

OptionWhat it suppliesCaveat
Regional RIMatching usage discount across AZs in a Region; eligible instance-size flexibilityNo capacity reservation
Zonal RIMatching discount + capacity reserved in one specified AZMust match reservation attributes; capacity availability subject to purchase; not multi-AZ HA
On-Demand Capacity ReservationReserve matching EC2 capacity in a chosen AZ independently of RI commitmentBilling discounts and capacity guarantees are separate decisions

Exam trigger. Need matching EC2 capacity in a particular AZ → a Zonal RI or an appropriate On-Demand Capacity Reservation; Regional RI alone is insufficient.

gp2 vs gp3, and what EC2 monitoring sees

gp2: baseline 3 IOPS/GiB, minimum 100 and maximum 16,000 IOPS; small volumes can burst using credits. A 100 GiB volume has 300 baseline IOPS, not a permanent 3,000 IOPS guarantee.

gp3: performance is provisioned independently of size, with a 3,000 IOPS / 125 MiB/s baseline; current general-purpose volume limits reach 80,000 IOPS / 2,000 MiB/s subject to volume size/IOPS ratios and the EC2 platform’s EBS bandwidth. Outposts has lower limits. Unlike gp2, gp3 does not use burst credits.

EC2 basic monitoring publishes most metrics every 5 minutes; detailed monitoring publishes them every 1 minute. NetworkOut is native. Guest RAM usage and filesystem/disk-space utilisation need the CloudWatch agent/custom metrics; native disk I/O metrics are not free-space utilisation.

Common trap. Detailed monitoring changes frequency, not the set of guest memory/filesystem metrics.

Replacement cutover: stable IP vs DNS redundancy

Think of it as: Keep the published phone number while moving it to a prepared office; some calls can drop during the transfer.

An Elastic IP is a static public IPv4 address allocated in one Region. Prepare/test instance B while A serves, then reassociate the EIP to B. Clients keep the address, but reassociation and connection recovery can briefly interrupt traffic; this is not guaranteed zero-downtime.

For a self-hosted authoritative DNS service that must keep its EC2 public IP, EIP reassociation can meet the address constraint. Route 53 DNS failover changes routing answers and has detection, TTL and resolver-cache effects; it does not automatically preserve that instance’s address. Independent authoritative nameservers improve resilience beyond one server.

Scroll the table horizontally on a narrow screen.

ApproachAvailability / addressComplexity
Stop, then build replacementLonger no-ready-server gap; auto public address may changeSimple but disruptive
Prepare replacement + move EIPSame public IPv4; brief cutover interruption possibleValidate replacement and handle reconnection
Multiple independent servers + DNS failoverRedundancy; detection/caching affect failover; multiple addressesMore infrastructure, health and DNS design

Exam trigger. Must preserve an EC2-hosted service’s public IPv4 while replacing the instance → consider EIP reassociation within its Region.

Common trap. Immutable replacement means a new deployment target; it does not itself guarantee continuous service or automatically move an EIP.

# Amazon Linux example; first-boot setup, not a recurring job.
dnf install -y nginx
systemctl enable --now nginx
