EC2 Auto Scaling

Maintain fleet capacity across AZs; pair with ELB to route traffic.

  • One ASG belongs to one Region and uses subnets in one or more AZs. It normally attempts to balance instances across enabled AZs.
  • The group replaces unhealthy instances and scales instance count in/out. Changing instance size is a separate vertical-scaling operation.
  • ELB distributes requests across registered targets. Its cross-zone setting controls whether an LB node can route outside its own AZ; it does not rebalance the instance fleet.

Decision boundary. Cross-zone ≠ cross-Region. An ASG and a regional load balancer stay within one Region. Use separate regional stacks plus Route 53 or Global Accelerator for global traffic routing.

Try min / max / desired / current capacity

2 instances in AZ A; 8 in AZ B

ASG balances instance capacity; ELB balances requests. This is an uneven snapshot of 10 healthy, equal-weight targets. Assume 100 requests/s, split equally between two load balancer nodes, with uniform routing and no stickiness.

One AWS Region · ap-southeast-2 · one regional load balancer

100 requests/s → LB node A (50) + LB node B (50)

Each LB node can send its share to all 10 targets across both AZs.

AZ A · 2 targets
10%10%

20% total · 20 requests/s

AZ B · 8 targets
10%10%10%10%10%10%10%10%

80% total · 80 requests/s

Cross-zone ON: 100% ÷ 10 = 10% per target. AZ A receives 20%; AZ B receives 80%.

Why 2 + 8? ASG normally tries to balance instances across enabled AZs; this could be a temporary imbalance. Changing ELB cross-zone routing does not move instances or change the ASG desired capacity.

Defaults. ALB enables cross-zone at the load balancer; a target group can disable it. NLB disables it by default. Actual shares depend on routing, health, weights and connections; the percentages above are an educational model.

Across Regions? Route 53 routing policies or Global Accelerator → separate regional load balancers → separate regional ASGs. Cross-zone means AZs within one Region; one ASG does not span Regions.

Which metric should drive target tracking?

Predefined metrics include ASGAverageCPUUtilization, ASGAverageNetworkIn, ASGAverageNetworkOut and ALBRequestCountPerTarget (with the target-group/load-balancer resource label). Pick a metric that changes appropriately as worker capacity changes.

EC2 NetworkOut counts bytes sent by the instance; ASGAverageNetworkOut is an aggregate target-tracking choice. SQS queue depth alone does not normalise for workers: use a custom/metric-math visible backlog per InService instance.

Target backlog per worker = acceptable delay / average processing time. With 60 s acceptable delay and 2 s/message, target 30 visible messages/worker. Handle zero workers explicitly; adding workers cannot fix a downstream bottleneck.

Exam trigger. Scale consumers from queue demand → backlog per worker, not CPU by default.

Common trap. ASG maintains capacity across configured AZs in one Region. It does not route requests or create multi-Region failover.

ASG configuration excerpt 
{
  "MinSize": 2,
  "DesiredCapacity": 10,
  "MaxSize": 20,
  "VPCZoneIdentifier": "subnet-az-a,subnet-az-b"
}

DesiredCapacity=10 sets the fleet total, not a 2/8 AZ allocation. A launch template supplies AMI, instance type, security groups and bootstrap configuration. Scale against the measured bottleneck.

Application Load Balancer

Route HTTP requests to healthy targets.

  • An internet-facing ALB routes HTTP requests to healthy targets, including targets with private IP addresses.
  • Health checks have their own path, port, matcher and network reachability; direct access can work while a target is unhealthy.
  • With cross-zone balancing and equal healthy target weights, 2 targets in AZ A + 8 in AZ B means about 10% per target.

Decision boundary. ALB access logs describe requests. CloudWatch metrics aggregate measurements. CloudTrail describes AWS API/account activity.

Who called /GetOrder, and where did the time go?

Client → ALB → private target → response. An access log records request-level evidence, including some requests that never reach a target. Logging must be enabled; delivery is best effort.

# Synthetic legacy-format entry; first 13 fields only.
# Wrapped for reading; a real entry is one line with more fields.
https 2026-10-29T01:00:00.200000Z app/orders/abc123
203.0.113.10:51500 10.0.2.15:8080
0.001 0.180 0.002 200 200 120 450
"GET https://api.example.com:443/GetOrder?orderId=o-42 HTTP/1.1"
Scroll the table horizontally to compare columns.
FieldExample → meaning
client:port / target:port203.0.113.10:51500 called target 10.0.2.15:8080. With an upstream proxy, the client field can be that proxy.
request_processing_time0.001 seconds from ALB receipt to dispatch toward the target
target_processing_time0.180 seconds until target response headers start; inspect backend work first
response_processing_time0.002 seconds from target headers reaching ALB until ALB starts sending the response
elb_status_code / target_status_code200 / 200: target replied and ALB returned success. 503 / - can indicate ALB had no usable target; check target health and routing.
request_lineHTTP method, URL/path/query and protocol; later fields include user agent, TLS details, actions and trace ID

Timing caveat. These fields describe different boundaries, not a full browser stopwatch. Upload/WAF behavior affects attribution; -1 can mean a processing phase could not complete. A trace ID helps correlate evidence but does not create downstream spans.

Delivery. Traditional access logging writes compressed files to S3 (disabled by default). Use a same-Region bucket and the required log-delivery bucket policy. AWS also supports the newer CloudWatch Logs integration, with destinations including CloudWatch Logs, Firehose and S3. Choose the delivery path deliberately; CloudWatch metrics are a separate signal.

QuestionEvidenceWhat it tells you
Which client, URL, status and target timing?ALB access logsRequest details; not the application body or a complete audit ledger
Is traffic/latency/error rate rising?CloudWatch metricsRequestCount, TargetResponseTime, HTTPCode_ELB_5XX_Count vs HTTPCode_Target_5XX_Count
Who changed a listener or security setting?CloudTrailAdministrative AWS API activity; not each HTTP request
Why is this target unhealthy?Target health reason + health-check/application logsCheck path, port, matcher, security groups and NACLs
Try it · ALB frontend and target routing

A public frontend can route to private targets; registering a target does not build network connectivity.

Change the scenario

Client → ALB DNS → listener → matching rule → target group → healthy target. Internal ALBs need private connectivity; private IP targets still need routes and network permissions.

Assumes valid DNS, ALB listener rules/SG, NACLs and target health. IP examples use permitted private ranges. Lambda invocation permission is assumed allowed; it is not a target TCP connection. Local learning model; no AWS requests.

Host/path rules, stickiness and uneven traffic

smart.com/api selects a path-pattern rule such as /api*; api.smart.com selects a host-header rule. They can also be combined. An ALB listener routes to a target group; its algorithm, healthy targets and connections determine the observed distribution.

ALB cross-zone is always enabled at load-balancer level, but can be disabled for supported target groups. Sticky sessions bind a client session to a target and can skew counts; they require cross-zone enabled. Unequal instance types do not automatically receive traffic in proportion to CPU/RAM.

Legacy Classic Load Balancer supports basic listener/backend routing, cookie stickiness and cross-zone settings, but lacks ALB host/path target-group rules. CLB uses round robin for TCP listeners and least outstanding requests for HTTP/HTTPS; ALB supports configurable target-group algorithms. Unequal instance types do not create automatic CPU-proportional target weights.

Exam trigger. Same hostname, different URL paths → ALB path rules; different subdomains → host rules.

Common trap. 2+8 targets → about 10% each is an idealised equal-weight example, not a guarantee of exactly equal request counts.

Listener → rule → target group → target

Think of it as: The public reception desk selects a department; the department’s target list gives the actual office address. A name on the list does not build a road there.

Flow. Client → ALB DNS endpoint → HTTPS listener :443 → host/path rule → target group → healthy backend.

An ALB belongs to one Region and VPC. An internet-facing ALB has public-facing endpoints; an internal ALB requires private connectivity. Both can forward to private backends. Listeners accept configured HTTP/HTTPS ports; listener rules choose a target group.

A host rule matches the HTTP Host header; it does not make “hostname” a target type. IP registration does not create peering, routes, security-group permissions, NACL rules or return paths. Reachable private IPs outside the VPC can be supported targets; publicly routable IPs cannot be registered as IP targets.

Scroll the table horizontally on a narrow screen.

Target typeDestinationBoundary
instancePrimary private IP of primary EC2 network interfaceRegister instance IDs in the ALB VPC
ipExact registered supported IP addressSame VPC or reachable supported private network; no public IP targets
lambdaLambda invocation through service APIFunction permission; not a target-subnet TCP connection

Exam trigger. Public frontend + private backend is normal. Other-VPC private IP → verify actual forward/return connectivity.

Common trap. Host-based routing is a listener rule, not a target type. Registration alone does not guarantee health or reachability.

Target-group health-check excerpt 
{
  "HealthCheckProtocol": "HTTP",
  "HealthCheckPort": "traffic-port",
  "HealthCheckPath": "/health",
  "Matcher": {"HttpCode": "200"}
}

Request tracing supplies an X-Amzn-Trace-Id for correlation; instrumentation is still needed for downstream spans. The 10% example assumes request-count routing, not differing target weights, stickiness or connection behaviour.

Amazon API Gateway

Expose an API with routing, integration and access controls.

  • A stage is a named environment pointing to an API deployment snapshot. A canary tests a newer deployment on the same stage URL.
  • Stage variables configure integrations; VTL mapping templates transform payloads. A proxy integration instead passes its standard event to the backend.
  • Authorizers establish caller access. Usage plans meter API-key consumers; caching can avoid repeated backend work.

Decision boundary. API keys are not authentication. Usage-plan quotas/throttles are best effort, not hard spend limits. Verify the API type before selecting a feature.

Follow one request: GET /GetOrder

Two stages of one REST API. The URL chooses the stage; the API key identifies the consuming application. This is a local illustration, not a live AWS call.

Application data plane · caller → API Gateway → Lambda 
GET https://a1b2c3d4e5.execute-api.ap-southeast-2.amazonaws.com/prod/GetOrder?orderId=o-42
Authorization: <Cognito access JWT>
x-api-key: <PartnerApp API key>

200 OK · prod → deployment d1 → orders:prod (version 1)

  1. URL → stage → deployment

    /prod selects prod, pointing to API deployment d1. /GetOrder is the resource; GET is the method.

  2. Who is calling?

    The Cognito authorizer validates the access token and required orders/read scope. The API key separately identifies PartnerApp for its usage plan.

  3. Validate input & apply usage limits

    Require orderId and an API key on this method. PartnerDemo targets 10 requests/s, burst 20, and 1,000/day per key across prod + beta.

  4. Cache → mapping → integration

    On a cache miss, a non-proxy VTL mapping creates the Lambda JSON below. The integration uses stage variable functionAlias=prod to invoke orders:prod.

  5. Backend → response

    Lambda checks that user-42 may read order o-42, loads the order, and returns 200. Integration/method response settings expose that result to the caller.

Mapped Lambda input · custom/non-proxy integration
{
  "orderId": "o-42",
  "environment": "prod",
  "callerSub": "user-42"
}
Caller receives
HTTP 200
{
  "orderId": "o-42",
  "status": "READY",
  "apiVersion": "v1"
}

prod: GET caching enabled, TTL 60 s, cache keys = Authorization + orderId. beta: cache disabled. A cache hit skips Lambda; it must never cross user/tenant boundaries.

Developer control plane. Deploy an API snapshot; point a stage to it; configure its variables, cache and logs. Here the integration target is orders:${stageVariables.functionAlias} (shorthand). prod → Lambda alias prod/v1; beta → alias beta/v2. Grant API Gateway permission to invoke those aliases. A stage, API deployment, and Lambda version are separate objects; stages do not automatically isolate code or data.

Custom domain. https://api.example.com/orders/GetOrder can map orders → this API's prod stage. The mapping selects the stage even when its name is absent from the public URL.

Evidence. Stage access/execution logs, CloudWatch metrics and enabled traces explain requests. CloudTrail records API configuration changes. The numbered checkpoints explain responsibilities, not a guaranteed internal execution order.

Assume successful API authentication; separately decide whether the caller may invalidate the cached response.

Change the scenario

Unexpired entry → cache hit. Authorised max-age=0 → backend fetch → replace entry. Unauthorised invalidation can be rejected or ignored according to configuration.

Method requires authorisation for invalidation; caller’s normal invoke permission is assumed allowed. “Unexpired” describes TTL, not guaranteed source-data freshness. REST API response cache only. Local learning model; no AWS requests.

Select a stage, then test caller, integration and execution permissions independently.

Change the example

Client → API authorisation → Gateway invoke permission → Lambda → execution-role permission → DynamoDB. A stage variable selects the function; it grants no access.

Same-account illustration, no explicit Deny, valid integration/alias/source-ARN scopes. The role toggle means the alternative integration credentials role is correctly configured. Other IAM controls are assumed satisfied. Local learning model; no AWS requests.

REST API integration types — MOCK has no backend

Scroll the table horizontally on a narrow screen.

REST integration typeWhat happensWhen to choose
MOCKAPI Gateway creates response from configured mappings/responsesContract tests/stubs; no Lambda/HTTP backend invoked
AWS_PROXYLambda proxy event → Lambda; function returns proxy responseNo custom VTL body transformation contract
AWSAWS service or Lambda custom integrationConfigure mappings and integration/method responses
HTTP_PROXYForward to HTTP endpoint with proxy behaviourBackend handles request/response contract
HTTPCustom HTTP integrationMapping templates/response mappings can transform payloads
 
// MOCK integration: conceptual configuration excerpts
requestTemplates: {"application/json": "{\"statusCode\": 200}"}
integrationResponse: {statusCode: "200", body: "{\"status\":\"stub\"}"}
// Configure the matching method response; no backend is called.

Exam trigger. Return a test response without calling any backend → MOCK.

Common trap. API Gateway API type matters: this is the REST API integration vocabulary; HTTP APIs have a different feature/API model.

HTTP anatomy and authorised cache refresh

Think of it as: A waiter can reuse an unexpired order slip; an authorised “check again” instruction asks the kitchen for a fresh answer.

Flow. GET /prod/GetOrder?id=42 → stage/method → cache key → cached response or backend → cache update.

With caching enabled, an appropriately authorised Cache-Control: max-age=0 request fetches a fresh integration response and updates that entry. Configure the method to require authorisation and grant execute-api:InvalidateCache to the caller. For unauthorised invalidation, configuration can return 403, ignore with a response warning, or ignore silently. Cross-account cache invalidation is not supported.

An unexpired cached response may still be stale relative to the source data. Expired/missing entries fetch from the backend normally. Cache keys must distinguish the response inputs and authorised data scope.

Scroll the table horizontally on a narrow screen.

Request partExampleResponsibility
Method + pathGET /prod/GetOrderAction/resource; prod selects the stage
Query string?id=42Request parameter; include relevant values in cache key
HeaderCache-Control: max-age=0REST API cache invalidation request
Body{"quantity":2} on a suitable POSTPayload; not a replacement for a header
 
# Executable curl shape; add configured authentication/signing as needed
curl -H "Cache-Control: max-age=0" \
  "https://API_ID.execute-api.ap-southeast-2.amazonaws.com/prod/GetOrder?id=42"
# Header alone does not grant execute-api:InvalidateCache.

Exam trigger. Refresh a REST API cached entry → Cache-Control: max-age=0 plus required permission/configuration.

Common trap. ?bypass_cache=1 and Bypass-Cache: 1 have no built-in invalidation meaning. HTTP APIs do not offer the same REST managed response cache.

Stage configuration vs three permission directions

Think of it as: The caller shows a ticket; the receptionist needs permission to call the office; the office worker needs permission to open the filing cabinet. Changing the office number grants none of those permissions.

  1. 1 · Client authorisation
  2. 2 · API Gateway invocation permission
  3. 3 · Lambda execution role
  4. 4 · DynamoDB action

A REST stage references a deployed API snapshot. Stage variables are stage-owned key/value configuration, similar to environment variables: dev: lambdaFunction=my-api-dev; prod: lambdaFunction=my-api-prod. An integration can interpolate the function name or alias. A variable selects a target; it grants no invocation permission.

Incoming authorisation: IAM uses signed requests (normally SigV4), Cognito User Pools validate configured user tokens/scopes, and Lambda authorisers run custom logic. HTTP APIs also support native JWT authorisers. STS is not a standalone API Gateway authoriser: a trusted caller may AssumeRole, receive temporary credentials, then sign an AWS_IAM API request.

For the backend hop, use a Lambda resource-policy Allow for apigateway.amazonaws.com, scoped by the appropriate execute-api source ARN and selected function/alias. Alternatively configure API Gateway to assume a trusted invocation role with lambda:InvokeFunction permission. Console-created integrations may add Lambda permission automatically; stage-variable targets still need matching grants.

Scroll the table horizontally on a narrow screen.

BoundaryMechanismWhat it permits
Client → API GatewayIAM/SigV4, Cognito or Lambda authoriser as configuredInvoke the API method; STS only supplies credentials for the IAM path
API Gateway → LambdaFunction resource policy OR configured IAM invocation rolelambda:InvokeFunction on the selected target
Lambda → DynamoDBLambda execution roleRequired DynamoDB actions on the table/index
 
# Integration target shorthand (not a complete ARN)
${stageVariables.lambdaFunction}

# Executable permission shape; substitute your IDs and target
aws lambda add-permission --function-name my-api-dev \
  --statement-id apigw-dev-get-order --action lambda:InvokeFunction \
  --principal apigateway.amazonaws.com \
  --source-arn 'arn:aws:execute-api:ap-southeast-2:111111111111:API_ID/dev/GET/GetOrder'
# For a qualified alias target, scope permission to the matching alias.

Exam trigger. API accepted caller but returns 500 before Lambda runs → inspect integration target and invoke permission. Lambda AccessDenied downstream → execution role.

Common trap. A Lambda execution role controls outgoing AWS calls, not who may invoke the function. For the alternative role path, both trust and permissions must be correct; explicit Deny still applies.

Create or import PartnerApp’s API key, then attach it to this plan separately. Mark GET /GetOrder as API Key Required. Both stages share this example’s per-key limits; the key does not route traffic. Quotas/throttles are best effort. Cache only safely scoped responses, with TTL/invalidation appropriate for changes in data and entitlements.

AWS Lambda

Execute event-driven code without operating a conventional server fleet.

  • For conventional Lambda compute, memory is 128–10,240 MB; CPU grows with memory, with about one vCPU at 1,769 MB.
  • Layers share code/dependencies and custom runtime content; they do not allocate extra CPU.
  • Published versions are immutable. $LATEST is unpublished. An alias points to a published version and can weight a second version.

Decision boundary. Call the alias to use its routing policy. An alias cannot point to another alias. A new version alone does not create a canary.

ControlPurposeDoes not mean
MemoryMemory + proportional CPUIndependent CPU selector for this compute mode
Reserved concurrencyReserve and cap function concurrencyWarm execution environments
Provisioned concurrencyPre-initialize environments for a version/aliasA newer deployed version
Weighted aliasProbabilistic split across two versionsExactly 10 of every 100 calls
Scaling: cold start vs concurrency vs CPU

On-demand Lambda automatically adds execution environments within scaling/concurrency quotas. Reserved concurrency reserves AND caps a function’s concurrency; it does not warm environments. Provisioned concurrency pre-initialises environments on a version/alias; excess requests can use on-demand capacity when allowed.

Application Auto Scaling can schedule provisioned concurrency before a known peak or target-track provisioned-concurrency utilisation for variable load. Scheduling is proactive; target tracking reacts and needs time to scale.

Cold-start latency → consider provisioned concurrency after measuring initialisation. CPU-heavy handler duration → increase memory (128–10,240 MB for standard functions; ~1 vCPU at 1,769 MB), profile and measure cost/duration. Warm environments do not supply extra per-invocation CPU.

Common trap. Reserved concurrency is not provisioned concurrency; neither a layer nor a warm environment fixes CPU starvation.

Invocation errors: who owns retry and the DLQ?

Scroll the table horizontally on a narrow screen.

PathRetry responsibilityFailure evidence
Synchronous InvokeCaller waits for result/error; caller or invoking service owns retryFunction error can be in a successful Invoke API response; inspect FunctionError/payload
Asynchronous InvokeLambda queue; default 2 retries for function errorsThrottle/system errors retry with backoff up to the event-age window (6 h default); duplicates possible
Async failure captureConfigure Lambda DLQ (SQS/SNS) or supported on-failure destinationDLQ stores failed event; destination adds invocation context; delivery also needs permissions
SQS event source mappingLambda polls queue and deletes successful workUse source queue redrive/DLQ; Lambda async-invocation DLQ is not this path

Common trap. A queue-triggered Lambda is not the same as InvocationType=Event.

Container/runtime and configuration contract

Lambda container images must be Linux, target one architecture (x86_64 or arm64), and stay within 10 GB uncompressed including layers. Multi-architecture images are not supported; a normal container image still needs Lambda-compatible invocation handling.

Runtime API is the HTTP contract to fetch invocations/report results. A Runtime Interface Client (RIC) implements that contract inside the image/runtime. The Runtime Interface Emulator (RIE) is a local testing proxy; it does not emulate IAM, AWS networking or all service behaviour.

Environment variables are strings with an aggregate 4 KB limit for a function. Store large configuration externally; use Secrets Manager/Parameter Store when appropriate rather than treating env vars as a secret-rotation system.

Exam trigger. CPU-intensive code → tune memory; large container dependencies → image packaging, still subject to Lambda quotas.

Node.js ZIP: declaring a dependency does not install it

Think of it as: A shopping list is not a pantry. Ship the ingredients, not only the list.

  1. 1 · Source + package lock
  2. 2 · CI: install / build
  3. 3 · ZIP / layer / image
  4. 4 · Runtime loads modules

package.json declares packages; node_modules/ contains their installed code. Lambda does not run npm install when you upload a ZIP. Install/build in development or CI, then ship the handler at the archive root with required dependencies. With an existing lockfile, npm ci provides a reproducible install.

A layer can provide dependencies separately (Node.js layers use the supported nodejs/node_modules path); a container image is another packaging model. Bundle the runtime/library versions you require explicitly, even when the runtime includes an SDK. Native modules must match the Lambda Linux runtime and architecture.

Scroll the table horizontally on a narrow screen.

ResponsibilityBuild timeRuntime
Dependenciesnpm install to update lockfile; npm ci --omit=dev in CIrequire("pg") loads already packaged driver
ApplicationPackage index.js and installed production dependenciesHandler executes; no automatic npm install
Database accessConfigure permissions, secrets and connectivity separatelyDriver connects to PostgreSQL; packaging does not create the database

Build commands (Bash), then index.js contents (JavaScript)

# Build commands inside a project containing index.js
npm install pg                 # once: update manifest + lockfile
npm ci --omit=dev               # CI: install from the committed lockfile
zip -r ../lambda.zip index.js package.json package-lock.json node_modules/
# ZIP root: index.js, manifests, node_modules/pg/ and its dependencies

// index.js — CommonJS example; configure DATABASE_URL securely
const { Client } = require('pg');
exports.handler = async () => {
  const db = new Client({ connectionString: process.env.DATABASE_URL });
  await db.connect();
  try { return (await db.query('SELECT 1 AS ok')).rows; }
  finally { await db.end(); }
};
// This simple connection-per-invocation example still needs DB network/auth setup.

Exam trigger. Cannot find module pg after ZIP upload → verify installed dependency files/layer and archive paths, not just package.json.

Common trap. npm ci needs a matching lockfile. Bundlers/layers can change the artifact shape, but required runtime code must still be present.

UpdateAlias request: v1 90%, v2 10% 
{
  "FunctionName": "orders",
  "Name": "prod",
  "FunctionVersion": "1",
  "RoutingConfig": {"AdditionalVersionWeights": {"2": 0.1}}
}

Rollback: remove additional weights and route prod to v1. Measure duration and cost together. Lambda Managed Instances has different compute configuration; do not generalize this memory-only rule to every Lambda offering.

AWS CloudFormation

Provision related resources as a versioned stack.

  • Resources is required. Parameters, Mappings, Conditions, Outputs and Transform are optional sections.
  • DependsOn is a resource attribute; there is no top-level Dependencies section. Ref/GetAtt also create implicit dependencies.
  • Conditions gate resources/outputs or property values through Fn::If. Parameters supply inputs; a Condition cannot be attached to a parameter.

Decision boundary. Export names are unique per account/Region. Standard Fn::ImportValue references stay in that account/Region; an active import prevents changing/deleting the exported value.

ExpressionMeaning
!RefParameter value or resource-specific return value
!GetAttResource attribute
!SubString substitution
!FindInMap [Map, TopKey, SecondKey]Mapping lookup, e.g. Region → AMI
!If [Condition, Yes, No]Conditional value
Valid parameters, Conditions vs DependsOn

Parameter types include **String, Number, List, CommaDelimitedList**, supported **AWS-specific types** (for example AWS::EC2::VPC::Id and List<AWS::EC2::Subnet::Id>), and supported **SSM parameter value types**. `DependentParameter` is not a valid type; native Boolean is not a parameter type either.

Conditions decide whether a resource/output is created or select a property through Fn::If. DependsOn controls ordering for resources that are created. It does not test an input or make a resource optional. References can create implicit dependencies.

Parameters:
  Stage:
    Type: String
    AllowedValues: [dev, prod]
Conditions:
  IsProd: !Equals [!Ref Stage, prod]
# Resource: Condition: IsProd → create only in prod.
# Resource: DependsOn: OtherResource → order, not a boolean check.
Pseudo parameters: AWS supplies deployment context

Think of it as: The form asks you for a name; the office supplies its address and the assigned case number.

Flow. CDK code → synth template → CloudFormation deploy → resolve account/Region/stack context.

Think of a template as a function: Parameters are user inputs; pseudo parameters are AWS-provided context. CloudFormation resolves references during stack deployment/evaluation, not as ordinary application compile-time constants.

CDK synthesis emits a CloudFormation template. Environment-aware CDK code can resolve some context earlier, but unresolved AWS references remain tokens for CloudFormation to resolve at deployment.

Scroll the table horizontally on a narrow screen.

Pseudo parameterValue
AWS::RegionDeployment Region
AWS::AccountIdDeployment account ID
AWS::StackNameStack name
AWS::StackIdUnique stack ARN
AWS::PartitionARN partition: aws, aws-cn, aws-us-gov, etc.
AWS::NoValueRemove a property when returned by Fn::If
 
# CloudFormation YAML excerpt
Outputs:
  Region:
    Value: !Ref AWS::Region
  Account:
    Value: !Ref AWS::AccountId
  Stack:
    Value: !Ref AWS::StackId
# Optional property pattern: !If [UseValue, value, !Ref AWS::NoValue]

Exam trigger. Need current account/Region without user input → pseudo parameter.

Common trap. AWS::NoValue removes a property through Fn::If; it is not an empty string or a parameter you declare.

Minimal conditional resource + export 
AWSTemplateFormatVersion: '2010-09-09'
Parameters:
  Environment:
    Type: String
    AllowedValues: [dev, prod]
Conditions:
  IsProd: !Equals [!Ref Environment, prod]
Resources:
  Orders:
    Type: AWS::SQS::Queue
    Properties:
      MessageRetentionPeriod: !If [IsProd, 1209600, 345600]
Outputs:
  QueueArn:
    Value: !GetAtt Orders.Arn
    Export:
      Name: !Sub '${AWS::StackName}-QueueArn'

StackSets deploy a template across selected accounts/Regions with parameters and permissions. This is different from a same-Region export/import dependency. Consult current docs for newer cross-Region output-reference features.

AWS reference: Template sections · Exports and imports · StackSets · Parameter types · Pseudo parameters

AWS CDK

Define AWS infrastructure using programming-language constructs.

  • Compose constructs into stacks/apps using TypeScript, JavaScript, Python, Java, C#/.NET or Go.
  • cdk synth produces CloudFormation templates; cdk deploy uses CloudFormation to create or update the stack.
  • Covers serverless and other infrastructure: Lambda, APIs, VPCs, EC2, ECS, databases and more. Reusable constructs can generate many resources.

Decision boundary. CDK is not a runtime and is not limited to servers. SAM and CDK both describe infrastructure; choose serverless YAML shorthand/local tooling versus general programming-language composition.

StepResponsibility
ConstructReusable infrastructure component in code
StackDeployment unit that maps to a CloudFormation stack
cdk synthGenerate CloudFormation; does not start a production application
cdk deployProvision/update the stack through CloudFormation
diff previews; deploy changes resources

cdk diff compares the synthesised stack with its deployed state and displays proposed differences; it does not apply the application update. Its default workflow may use a temporary CloudFormation change set for replacement accuracy.

cdk deploy provisions/updates through CloudFormation. Neither command runs your business application locally; the provisioned Lambda/EC2/ECS resources execute it.

Exam trigger. Review proposed infrastructure changes → diff; apply reviewed changes → deploy.

CDK stack excerpt · creates a Lambda function 
from aws_cdk import Stack, aws_lambda as lambda_
from constructs import Construct

class OrdersStack(Stack):
    def __init__(self, scope: Construct, construct_id: str, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(scope, construct_id, **kwargs)
        lambda_.Function(self, "Orders",
            runtime=lambda_.Runtime.PYTHON_3_13,
            handler="app.handler",
            code=lambda_.Code.from_asset("src"))

cdk init → write constructs → build if needed → cdk synth → cdk deploy. SAM can also declare ordinary CloudFormation resources; serverless scope versus broad infrastructure is a preference, not an absolute capability boundary.

AWS reference: CDK concepts · CDK synthesis · CDK diff

AWS SAM

Define, build, test and deploy a serverless application.

  • The SAM template extends CloudFormation; Transform: AWS::Serverless-2016-10-31 expands shorthand into deployable resources.
  • The SAM CLI builds/packages code, invokes supported functions locally, emulates supported API routes and deploys through CloudFormation.
  • Mix AWS::Serverless::* shorthand with standard AWS::* resources in the same template. The resulting Lambda functions/API/database run in AWS.

Decision boundary. SAM is infrastructure and development tooling, not compute. AWS::Serverless::UserPool is invalid; use AWS::Cognito::UserPool. Local testing does not reproduce every cloud behavior.

Common shorthand resourceWhat it defines
AWS::Serverless::FunctionLambda function + supported events, permissions and deployment settings
AWS::Serverless::ApiAPI Gateway REST API
AWS::Serverless::HttpApiAPI Gateway HTTP API
AWS::Serverless::SimpleTableA DynamoDB table with simplified configuration
AWS::Serverless::StateMachineStep Functions state machine
AWS::Serverless::LayerVersionLambda layer version
AWS::Serverless::ApplicationNested/reusable serverless application, including SAR applications
sam sync vs sam deploy: feedback loop vs managed release

Scroll the table horizontally on a narrow screen.

CommandPathRecovery boundary
sam sync --code / --watchFast development loop; supported code updates use service APIs directly; other changes can use CloudFormationDo not assume a stack rollback reverses direct code syncs
sam deployPackages/deploys a CloudFormation-managed update/change setNormal stack failure/rollback behaviour unless explicitly disabled; use versioned artifacts for release
Production releaseRepeatable stack deployment + tested versions/aliases/hooks as appropriateUse sync in a development stack, not as a replacement for controlled promotion

Common trap. sam sync is not exclusively API-only: unsupported/code-independent infrastructure changes can trigger a CloudFormation deployment.

AWS Serverless Application Repository

Find, share and deploy versioned reusable serverless applications.

  • Applications package a SAM template with deployment artifacts; choose an application version and supply its parameters.
  • Publish privately for a team/organization or publicly, subject to sharing permissions.
  • AWS::Serverless::Application can reference a repository application; deployment creates the underlying application resources.

Decision boundary. SAR is an application repository, not compute. Service Catalog governs approved products; AWS Marketplace distributes third-party software/services.

Amazon DynamoDB

Key-value/document storage organized around key-based access.

  • GameName + Version identifies a game version; querying GameName returns its versions. Category + GameName on a GSI supports category lookup.
  • A GSI only returns projected attributes; use ALL when the index must return every game attribute. GSI reads are eventually consistent.
  • TTL is a Number containing Unix seconds. Expiration is asynchronous cleanup; TTL deletions can appear in Streams. Filter expired data when required.

Decision boundary. Read-then-write can race. Use an atomic conditional write for a request ID, then coordinate status/results with business side effects.

Transfer a voucher: fail the second write

CapacityBest starting clueWatch
On-demandVariable / uncertain request volumeHot keys and service quotas still apply
ProvisionedPredictable load; set read/write capacityThrottle if capacity is insufficient; consider Auto Scaling
Try it · DynamoDB RCU/WCU calculator

Round the item size first, then apply consistency and requests per second.

Change the scenario

12 KB → 3 read-size units × 0.5 × 16 reads/s = 24 RCUs. One normal 12 KB write/s needs 12 WCUs.

Successful single-item operations, equally sized items, no secondary-index write costs. Whole provisioned settings have a minimum of 1 RCU and 1 WCU; this is arithmetic sizing before headroom. Local learning model; no AWS requests.

Try it · Choose the cache boundary

Choose for the deciding requirement; another technology can be technically possible with more application work.

Change the example

DAX simplifies eligible DynamoDB read caching; Redis supports general-purpose cached values; CloudFront serves cacheable HTTP content. Strong reads bypass cached copies.

Choices describe a typical fit, not exclusive technical possibilities. Session durability/expiry and tenant-level authorisation still need application design. Local learning model; no AWS requests.

Try it · CLI projection, filtering and pagination

Use Users for attributes/filters, or switch to 250 S3 objects to see 100 → 100 → 50 output pages.

Change the example

Users: --page-size 4 and --max-items 5 can require two underlying calls. Projection/filtering change output, not the cost of evaluating the same records. The CLI NextToken resumes with --starting-token.

Fixed illustrative dataset order; actual DynamoDB Scan order is not guaranteed. Service pages are below 1 MB. Cursor handling is simplified, including intra-page resume; tokens are simulated and never sent to AWS. Changing dataset resets options/tokens. Local learning model; no AWS requests.

Try it · GSI capacity and write back-pressure

Compare base-table writes with the additional index-entry writes and eventual index reads.

Change the example

100 new 3 KB items/s need 300 table WCUs. One 1.5 KB GSI entry per item adds 200 index WCUs; a 150-WCU index can back-pressure table writes. Forty eventual index reads/s use 20 RCUs at this size.

Provisioned mode, one GSI, successful new eligible items, one index write per base write, no changed index keys/transactions or burst/adaptive headroom. Each Query evaluates/retrieves one projected entry; multi-entry Query size aggregation differs. KB = 1,024 bytes. It is sizing arithmetic, not an exact throttle predictor. Local learning model; no AWS requests.

Atomic transaction vs batch vs a recent read

Scroll the table horizontally on a narrow screen.

OperationContractDeciding boundary
TransactWriteItemsUp to 100 distinct items; aggregate item size ≤4 MB; same account/RegionPut/Update/Delete/ConditionCheck; whole bundle succeeds or cancels
BatchWriteItemUp to 25 Put/Delete operations; request ≤16 MBIndividual writes atomic; bundle not atomic; retry UnprocessedItems with backoff
Strong GetItem / QuerySupported table/LSI reads with ConsistentRead=trueRecent committed item data; not a multi-item transaction; no strong GSI reads
Conditional PutItemattribute_not_exists(primary_key)Prevents replacing that existing key atomically
Atomic ADD / arithmetic UpdateItemOne item updated without a read-then-write raceNot inherently idempotent; retry can increment twice

Exam trigger. Debit game credits + grant the purchased item, all-or-nothing → transaction with conditions for the business invariants.

Common trap. An awaited/synchronous batch can partially succeed. An async application can submit an atomic transaction; timing and atomicity are independent.

Capacity, hot partitions and scaling

Provisioned capacity is the configured budget; Auto Scaling changes that budget in response to utilisation, with reaction time. Adaptive capacity reallocates available capacity towards unevenly accessed partitions; it cannot create unlimited table/partition capacity or rescue every single hot key.

Distribute high-volume access across partition keys. Adding total WCU/RCU or switching to on-demand is not a universal cure for a hot item. For a voucher, condition the owner/balance update and use a transaction across ownership items.

// UpdateItem excerpt: atomic increment, NOT retry-idempotent
{"UpdateExpression":"ADD Views :one",
 "ExpressionAttributeValues":{":one":{"N":"1"}}}

Exam trigger. Hot key despite available table capacity → inspect key distribution and per-partition pressure, not only total WCU.

Read/write capacity: round size, then apply the rate

Think of it as: Buy capacity in rounded cartons: a partly filled carton still costs one carton; read consistency changes its price.

Flow. Item bytes → round to 4 KB read / 1 KB write units → consistency/transaction multiplier → requests per second.

Strong reads return the latest successfully committed data; eventual reads can be stale and consume half the read capacity, not two reads. The calculator models successful single-item reads/writes of equally sized items; KB here means 1,024 bytes, including attribute names and values.

12 KB × 16 eventual reads/s: ceil(12/4) = 3 size units; 3 × 0.5 = 1.5 units/read; 1.5 × 16 = 24 RCUs. Consumed units describe operations; provisioned units describe throughput per second. On-demand uses analogous request-unit arithmetic rather than provisioned RCU/WCU settings.

Scroll the table horizontally on a narrow screen.

OperationPer item-size chunkThen multiply by
Normal write1 write unit per 1 KB, rounded upWrites/s → WCUs
Strong read1 read unit per 4 KB, rounded upReads/s → RCUs
Eventual read0.5 read unit per 4 KB, rounded upReads/s → RCUs
Transactional read2 read units per 4 KB, rounded upReads/s → RCUs
Transactional write2 write units per 1 KB, rounded upWrites/s → WCUs

Exam trigger. Round item size before multiplying by request rate; transactions cost twice the equivalent strong-read/normal-write capacity.

Common trap. This single-item formula is not a universal Query/Scan estimator. Index writes, updates, condition failures and actual access distribution can add considerations; provision headroom.

LSI vs GSI: another access path, not a reordered table

Think of it as: Two library catalogues: LSI keeps the same reader’s drawer with a new sort order; GSI provides a separate set of drawers by another key.

Flow. Orders base UserID + OrderID → LSI UserID + OrderDate; GSI OrderStatus + OrderDate.

Like a relational index, an index offers a different lookup order. It does not physically reorder the original table. An LSI is not necessarily a simple pointer: it stores index keys and projected attributes. “Local” refers to sharing the table partition key and related storage organisation; GSI storage/partitioning is separate.

The 10 GB LSI item-collection limit applies per partition-key value to the base-table items plus their LSI entries. Creating LSIs only with the table is a DynamoDB design constraint, not a rule for all databases. A newly added GSI backfills existing eligible items before becoming active.

Provisioned accounting: LSI reads/writes share the table budget. GSI queries use the index’s eventual-read RCUs, not table RCUs. Writes to eligible base items can also write index entries; their sizes/changed keys determine the extra WCUs. Insufficient GSI write capacity can back-pressure base writes. Separate index reads, writes and storage add cost, but a suitable GSI can replace expensive repeated scans.

Scroll the table horizontally on a narrow screen.

BoundaryLSIGSI
Partition / sort keysSame partition key; alternative sort keyCan use different partition and sort keys
CreatedOnly with tableWith table or later (backfill)
Read consistencyStrong or eventualEventual only
Provisioned capacityShares base tableSeparate index capacity when provisioned
Storage/limit10 GB item collection per partition-key valueSeparate index partitions; no LSI item-collection limit
Write amplificationIncluded in table capacity accountingAdditional writes for affected index entries; changing an index key may delete old + insert new
Read sourceTable/LSI budget; non-projected attributes may require table fetchProjected index data only; use GSI RCUs

Exam trigger. Existing table needs a new lookup partition key → GSI. Same partition key + strong reads on another sort key → plan an LSI at table creation.

Common trap. Global means a different table-wide access path, not a cross-Region index.

Query vs Scan vs Parallel Scan

Think of it as: Query goes to the right filing drawer; Scan checks every drawer; Parallel Scan gives several clerks different portions of the filing room.

Flow. Suitable table/index partition key → Query. Otherwise Scan → process page → follow LastEvaluatedKey; parallel workers scan separate logical segments.

CLI view: projection chooses attributes (columns); filtering chooses returned items (rows), after reads. For the same evaluated data, neither reduces Scan capacity. CLI output pagination is separate from DynamoDB’s service-level LastEvaluatedKey/ExclusiveStartKey. Use the playground above for both Users and a 250-object S3 listing.

Scroll the table horizontally on a narrow screen.

OperationAccess patternCapacity / caveat
QueryPartition-key equality; optional sort-key conditionAn existing suitable table/index key may already suffice
ScanEvaluate table/index items, up to 1 MB per pageFilterExpression and ProjectionExpression do not reduce Scan read capacity
Parallel ScanConcurrent Segment workers with the same TotalSegmentsCan reduce elapsed time, but increases simultaneous read pressure
CLI projection / filter--projection-expression / --filter-expressionReturn fewer attributes/items; same evaluated data still costs reads
CLI service batching--page-sizeItems requested/evaluated per service call; DynamoDB can stop sooner at 1 MB
CLI output limit--max-itemsMaximum output items across automatic service calls
CLI resume--starting-tokenPass the CLI response NextToken unchanged; not a generic --next-token input
 
# Pseudocode: four concurrent workers; each paginates independently
def worker(segment):
    start = None
    while True:
        page = scan(TableName="Orders", Segment=segment,
                    TotalSegments=4, ExclusiveStartKey=start) # omit key initially
        process(page["Items"])
        start = page.get("LastEvaluatedKey")
        if not start: break
run_concurrently(worker, segments=range(4))

# Executable AWS CLI shape; aliases avoid reserved attribute names
aws dynamodb scan --table-name Users \
  --projection-expression "UserID, #n" \
  --filter-expression "#a = :yes" \
  --expression-attribute-names '{"#n":"Name","#a":"Active"}' \
  --expression-attribute-values '{":yes":{"BOOL":true}}' \
  --page-size 4 --max-items 5
# Resume using the returned CLI NextToken: --starting-token "TOKEN"

Exam trigger. No suitable key/index and a one-off full-table job → Scan; use Parallel Scan only when concurrency and capacity budget fit.

Common trap. A filter runs after reads. Segments are logical scan work, not a promise of one worker per physical partition; pagination still applies.

DAX vs Redis vs CloudFront: cache the right boundary

Think of it as: DAX is a DynamoDB-aware librarian; Redis is a general-purpose shelf you organise; CloudFront is a worldwide HTTP delivery depot.

  1. 1 · Application request
  2. 2 · DAX / Redis lookup, or HTTP CDN
  3. 3 · Source on miss

DAX shares eligible DynamoDB item/query results across clients; it is not a separate cache per signed-in user. Reuse depends on keys and query inputs. A DAX-compatible SDK/client and cluster endpoint handle lookup, population and much of the cache lifecycle. Cache hits are eventually consistent; strong reads pass through to DynamoDB and do not populate the cache.

Redis can cache DynamoDB data. Your application controls lookup, miss handling, population, TTL and invalidation. Choose it for custom keys, session data or computed values. For static S3 images, use CloudFront in the HTTP delivery path. Always preserve authorisation/tenant scope; a shared cache is not an entitlement check.

Scroll the table horizontally on a narrow screen.

CacheIntegration / responsibilityChoose when
DAXDAX client → cluster → DynamoDB; item/query cache logic largely managedRepeated eventual DynamoDB reads, minimal cache plumbing
ElastiCache RedisApplication → cache → any suitable source; application manages consistencySessions, database results or computed recommendations
CloudFrontBrowser → edge cache → HTTP origin such as S3Static assets and appropriate cacheable HTTP responses
Strong-read requirementBypass cache → DynamoDB table/LSILatest successfully committed data; a GSI cannot serve strong reads

Exam trigger. Repeated DynamoDB products + least cache logic → DAX. Arbitrary sessions/computation → Redis. S3 images → CloudFront.

Common trap. DAX does not provide strong cache hits; it can forward strong reads. Redis is capable of caching DynamoDB, but is not a direct CDN replacement.

{
  "TableName": "RequestLedger",
  "Item": {
    "RequestId": {"S": "req-42"},
    "Status": {"S": "IN_PROGRESS"},
    "ExpiresAt": {"N": "1793318400"}
  },
  "ConditionExpression": "attribute_not_exists(RequestId)"
}

The key schema must make RequestId the primary key in this separate ledger. A successful claim does not prove the payment/write completed; persist outcomes and recover abandoned work. A String Version sorts lexically; use Number or suitable encoding for numeric ordering.

Amazon SQS

Buffer work so consumers can process it independently.

  • Receive hides a message; DeleteMessage acknowledges success. Default visibility is 30 seconds, maximum 12 hours; duplicates still require idempotency.
  • PurgeQueue removes messages and keeps the queue. DeleteQueue removes both. RemovePermission edits queue-policy permission.
  • Choose queue type at creation; it cannot be converted later. Source and DLQ types must match. Queue tags are case-sensitive.

Decision boundary. VisibilityTimeout hides received work; DelaySeconds postpones initial availability; MessageRetentionPeriod limits retention. They are different clocks.

TypeDelivery / orderUse when
StandardAt least once; best-effort orderHigh throughput, order not required
FIFOOrdered within a message group; producer deduplicationOrdering/deduplication required; consumers remain idempotent
Try it · FIFO group order vs duplicate sends

Send two users’ operations, receive their group heads, and compare retries before and after five minutes.

Change the example

Per-user groups can progress independently. Reusing a send deduplication ID inside five minutes is acknowledged without adding another deliverable message, even after the first is deleted.

Queue-wide deduplication scope, one active head per group and successful DeleteMessage on completion. Content-hash equality is simulated; real SQS uses SHA-256 of body, excluding attributes. An explicit ID overrides content-based generation in real SQS. Local learning model; no AWS requests.

Polling, in-flight messages and large payloads

Stored messages are waiting in the queue; in-flight messages have been received but not deleted. Standard queues have an approximately 120,000 in-flight limit depending on traffic/backlog; FIFO currently supports 120,000. There is no fixed count quota on stored backlog, but retention and service quotas still apply.

Short polling (WaitTimeSeconds=0) samples servers and may return false-empty results. Long polling (1–20 s) queries all servers and waits for messages, reducing empty responses. At the Standard in-flight limit, short polling can return OverLimit; long polling waits without returning more messages until slots free.

Native messages are now up to 1 MiB (1,048,576 bytes), not the older 256 KB. The Java/Python SQS Extended Client stores large payloads in S3 (up to 2 GB) and queues a reference. Consumers need S3 permissions and coordinated object cleanup; this is not a native multi-GB queue body.

Visibility is a processing lease, not deletion. For Lambda polling SQS, configure the source queue redrive policy/DLQ. Lambda async-invocation retry/DLQ settings apply to its separate asynchronous queue, not SQS event source mappings.

Exam trigger. Excess empty receives → long polling; repeated processing → inspect visibility, failures and idempotency.

Common trap. Increasing stored backlog is not identical to hitting the in-flight limit.

Message encryption: service-side vs client-side

Think of it as: The queue locks its storage room for you; client-side encryption puts a separately locked box inside that room.

Flow. Authorised producer → TLS → SQS encrypts message body at rest → SQS decrypts → authorised consumer over TLS.

SSE-KMS uses envelope encryption: SQS manages data-key use, not the producer’s application logic. Producers generally need kms:GenerateDataKey + kms:Decrypt; consumers need kms:Decrypt for relevant keys. Check the key policy and service integrations too.

See IAM identity vs queue policies for who may call SendMessage/ReceiveMessage. Secrets Manager stores secrets; it is not the service encrypting queue storage.

Scroll the table horizontally on a narrow screen.

ChoiceWho encrypts at rest?Application / permission impact
SSE-SQSSQS with SQS-managed keysTransparent service encryption; no KMS key permissions
SSE-KMSSQS using KMS-protected data keysUsually unchanged Send/Receive code; check IAM and KMS permissions
Client-side encryptionYour application before SendMessageRequires encrypt/decrypt code and its own key-access model
HTTPS/TLSTransport layer, not queue storageProtects data in transit; not an at-rest alternative

Exam trigger. Encrypt SQS messages at rest with KMS and minimal application change → SSE-KMS with appropriate permissions.

Common trap. SSE does not mean the consumer must implement local decryption. Client-side encryption can add confidentiality but changes the application.

FIFO: group orders work; deduplication identifies a send

Think of it as: MessageGroupId chooses the checkout lane; MessageDeduplicationId is the receipt number that identifies one logical purchase.

  1. 1 · Producer sets group + operation ID
  2. 2 · FIFO suppresses duplicate sends
  3. 3 · Consumers process each group in order

The five-minute deduplication history can outlive receiving/deleting the original message. Suppression does not delete an already queued message, and a retry outside the window can enqueue again. FIFO ordering and send deduplication do not make business side effects exactly once: visibility expiry, failures and retries still require application idempotency.

FieldResponsibilityExample / trap
MessageGroupIdProducer chooses the ordering boundaryuser_id → one user’s ordered work; different users/groups can proceed concurrently
MessageDeduplicationIdProducer identifies one logical sendtransaction_id; repeat within five minutes is acknowledged without another deliverable message
ContentBasedDeduplicationSQS hashes message body using SHA-256Attributes are excluded; an explicitly supplied deduplication ID overrides the generated ID
ReceiveRequestAttemptIdIdentifies certain FIFO ReceiveMessage retriesReceive-side retry handling, not producer send deduplication
MessageOrderId / MessageHashNot real SQS parametersDo not substitute these for group/deduplication IDs
 
// SendMessage JSON excerpt
{"QueueUrl":"https://sqs.ap-southeast-2.amazonaws.com/111111111111/orders.fifo",
 "MessageBody":"{\"operation\":\"purchase\"}",
 "MessageGroupId":"user-42", "MessageDeduplicationId":"transaction-901"}

Exam trigger. Per-user order → MessageGroupId=user_id. Retry the same purchase → same logical deduplication ID within the window.

Common trap. A new random ID on every retry defeats explicit send deduplication. Same body with different attributes still hashes identically in content-based mode.

  "QueueUrl": "https://sqs.ap-southeast-2.amazonaws.com/123456789012/orders",
  "MaxNumberOfMessages": 10,
  "WaitTimeSeconds": 20,

Backlog per worker = ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible / running workers. Target backlog = acceptable wait / average processing time. Apply target tracking to ECS with an appropriate task-count metric and a scale-from-zero strategy.

Kinesis Data Streams

Retain continuous events in shard lanes for independent, replayable reads.

  • A stream contains shards; shards contain records. Partition keys map records to a shard, where Kinesis assigns sequence numbers.
  • PutRecords batches records. HTTP 200 can include partial failures: inspect FailedRecordCount and each result; retry only failed entries with backoff and jitter.
  • ProvisionedThroughputExceededException indicates capacity/hot-key pressure; InternalFailure is a service-side record error. Preserve an application event ID for deduplication.

Decision boundary. Spreading partition keys can fix a hot shard. Increasing provisioned shards can add capacity; merging shards or sending more requests does not fix producer throttling.

Records flow through shards

A record is one event: a data blob + partition key, assigned a sequence number when accepted. A shard is an ordered lane of records with its own throughput capacity. A stream contains those lanes. A record belongs to one shard; the shard is not a batch sent to the consumer.

Example. Devices send readings continuously. Each record totals 4 KiB = 4,096 bytes, including its partition key, before base64 encoding. The sample below illustrates sustained provisioned capacity, without producer aggregation or burst allowances.

1 · Producer300 records/s × 4 KiB = 1.172 MiB/sPutRecord / PutRecords · IAM-authorized writes

↓ Partition-key hash → shard hash range

2 · AWS Kinesis stream · telemetry · one Region

Many keys are assumed evenly distributed in this model. With one shard, all records still enter that lane.

Shard 1Incoming: 300 records/s · 1.172 MiB/s
r1r2r3…→
Demand: 117% of byte budget · 30% of record budget · over capacity

↓ Read records from each shard; track progress per shard

3 · Consumer applicationProcess accepted readings → update dashboard / store resultsGetRecords polling or enhanced fan-out · IAM-authorized reads

Aggregate: 1.172 MiB/s offered / 1 MiB/s shard-sum budget (117%). Each lane must fit independently.

300 records/s exceed one shard's sustained byte budget. Some writes can be throttled; retry failed records with backoff and jitter.

Per shard: min(1,000 records/s, 1,024 KiB/s ÷ 4 KiB) = 256 records/s. At 300 records/s, at least 2 evenly loaded shards are needed before headroom.

Two limits, one lane. Each shard supports sustained writes up to 1 MiB/s and 1,000 records/s; whichever is reached first limits you. At 4 KiB, bytes win. With 512-byte records, the record-count limit would win. These are rates, not the shard's total storage size.

Reading is independent. Shared-throughput consumers share up to 2 MiB/s per shard; enhanced fan-out provides up to 2 MiB/s per shard per registered consumer. Reading does not delete records. Retention controls replay; there is no global order across shards. PutRecords retries can also change producer event order.

Two consumers replaying 1.5 MiB/s each demand 3 MiB/s from the same shard's 2 MiB/s shared read budget. Enhanced fan-out gives each registered reader its own 2 MiB/s budget; it does not increase producer capacity.

Replay demand above is independent of the arrival-rate example: consumers can read older retained records. Shared polling also has a limit of 5 GetRecords calls/s per shard. Retention defaults to 24 hours and can extend to 365 days.

Capacity ≠ retention. The lane continues accepting records over time; it does not fill at 1 MiB and move to the next shard. Control-plane scaling changes the shard layout; data-plane calls write/read records. On-demand manages capacity for you, but a hot partition key still needs attention.

Capacity modeWho manages capacityWatch
ProvisionedYou set shard countPer-shard throughput / hot partition keys
On-demandService scales stream capacityScaling boundaries, hot keys and quotas still apply
Try it · KCL shard leases and workers

A worker can own several shard leases; extra workers do not create more shards.

Change the example

Ten shards and twenty one-worker instances → ten active workers and ten without shard leases within one application. Each independent application has its own lease/checkpoint set.

Even, settled lease assignment; one KCL worker per instance is an assumption, not an EC2 rule. Real balancing/recovery is dynamic. Multiple applications still share normal read limits unless using eligible dedicated fan-out. Local learning model; no AWS requests.

Shard budgets, hot keys and read contention

Think of it as: Ten checkout lanes do not help if every customer queues at lane one.

Flow. Producer partition key → hash range → one shard’s write budget; consumers later share/read that shard’s separate read budget.

For sustained provisioned writes, each shard has up to 1 MiB/s and 1,000 records/s. Ten evenly used shards provide up to 10 MiB/s aggregate byte throughput. Spare capacity on other shards is not a common pool for a hot shard.

A partition key hashes to one shard. Many well-spread keys can exploit additional/split shards; a single hot key still stays together. Reducing shard count cannot solve hot-key pressure. Retry only failed PutRecords entries with exponential backoff and jitter, then address capacity/key distribution.

Shared consumers share 2 MiB/s and 5 GetRecords calls/s per shard; enhanced fan-out gives each registered consumer up to 2 MiB/s per shard. This isolates read throughput, not producer write pressure or slow processing. Reads do not delete records: 24 h default retention, extendable to 365 days, enables replay with independent consumer positions.

Scroll the table horizontally on a narrow screen.

SignalTypical boundaryInvestigate
ProvisionedThroughputExceededExceptionData-plane throughput exceededWrite shard/record rate or shared read pressure; inspect the failing operation
LimitExceededExceptionService quota/control-plane operation limitAccount/Region quota or API-operation limit; inspect the API/error context

Exam trigger. Low aggregate utilisation + one saturated shard → partition-key skew. Shared consumer read contention → enhanced fan-out, not more producer retries.

Common trap. Shard-count quotas vary by Region/account and can change; LimitExceededException does not inherently mean “one shard is full”.

Streams vs delivery vs continuous analytics

ElastiCache, DynamoDB and RDS are not native Firehose destination types. To write there, build a suitable consumer/custom integration with its own retries, throughput and transaction handling; an arbitrary HTTP endpoint does not make them native destinations.

Scroll the table horizontally on a narrow screen.

ServiceResponsibilityChoose for
Kinesis Data StreamsRetained log with producers, shard lanes and independent consumersReplay/event processing; consumers own read progress
Amazon Data FirehoseBuffered managed delivery to a configured destinationS3, Redshift (stage in S3 then COPY), OpenSearch, Splunk, Iceberg and supported HTTP/partner destinations
Amazon Managed Service for Apache FlinkStateful streaming computation, windows, joins and aggregationsFormerly Kinesis Data Analytics for Apache Flink; separate from the retired SQL-app offering

Exam trigger. Deliver buffered records to S3 with minimal consumer code → Firehose. Compute continuous windowed analytics → Flink. Independent retained replay → Data Streams.

KCL workers: shard leases are the unit of ownership

Think of it as: A worker holds the checkout-lane assignment; one worker can cover several lanes, but twenty workers cannot invent twenty lanes in a ten-lane store.

  1. 1 · Shards
  2. 2 · Per-application leases
  3. 3 · Worker record processors
  4. 4 · Checkpoint / recovery

Within one consumer application, KCL assigns each shard lease to one active worker in steady state. One worker can run record processors for several shards. With 10 shards and 20 one-worker EC2 instances, at most 10 workers perform shard-level work concurrently in this simplified model; the rest cannot create extra shard parallelism.

Separate application identities have independent lease/checkpoint sets and can each consume the stream. This does not create more stream write capacity; shared-read throughput or enhanced fan-out limits still apply. Lease recovery and checkpoints do not eliminate duplicate processing after failures.

Exam trigger. More EC2 consumers than shards in one KCL app → no extra shard-level parallelism. Independent apps are a different boundary.

Common trap. A shard lease is not a shard copied to a worker. This is steady-state assignment, not an exactly-once side-effect guarantee.

PutRecords response: retry the second input record 
{
  "FailedRecordCount": 1,
  "Records": [
    {"SequenceNumber": "101", "ShardId": "shardId-000000000000"},
    {"ErrorCode": "ProvisionedThroughputExceededException",
     "ErrorMessage": "Rate exceeded"}
  ]
}

Results align with request order. PutRecords does not guarantee ordering across successful and retried records. Reducing readers does not directly fix producer-side write throttling.

Amazon ECS

Orchestrate container tasks and services; choose their compute separately.

  • ECS schedules tasks/services. A task definition is the container blueprint; a service maintains the desired tasks. EC2 and Fargate are distinct capacity choices.
  • Task-local ephemeral/bind-mount data is suitable for temporary files. EC2 host volumes depend on host lifecycle.
  • EFS provides persistent shared network files for supported ECS/Fargate tasks across AZs. Configure mount targets, NFS access and file permissions.

Decision boundary. A local volume is not a shared cross-AZ filesystem. Fargate EFS support requires a supported Linux platform; do not assume every OS/launch mode supports it.

NeedChooseLifecycle
Temporary task filesEphemeral storage / supported bind mountTask/host dependent
Shared persistent filesEFSIndependent of task replacement
Host configuration controlECS on EC2You manage host capacity
Managed container computeFargateTask CPU/memory allocation
ECS container instance registration vs EC2 lifecycle

For ECS on EC2, the ECS agent registers a container instance with the cluster. Drain it before planned termination to stop placing tasks and replace service tasks appropriately.

Terminating a running EC2 container instance with a connected agent normally deregisters it automatically. Stopped instances or disconnected agents can leave stale registrations requiring manual deregistration.

Deregistering an ECS container instance does not terminate the EC2 instance or stop its billing. Forced deregistration can orphan running tasks. These are EC2 host concerns, not a Fargate host-management procedure.

Common trap. The ECS cluster inventory and the underlying billable EC2 fleet are separate resources.

Task-definition storage excerpt 
{
  "volumes": [{
    "name": "shared",
    "efsVolumeConfiguration": {
      "fileSystemId": "fs-example",
      "transitEncryption": "ENABLED"
    }
  }],
  "containerDefinitions": [{
    "name": "worker", "image": "example/worker:1",
    "mountPoints": [{"sourceVolume": "shared", "containerPath": "/data"}]
  }]
}

The excerpt omits task roles, CPU/memory, networking and other required task settings. Add an EFS access point/IAM authorization where needed; a mount declaration alone does not grant access.

AWS Fargate

Supply managed compute capacity for containers without managing EC2 hosts.

  • For ECS, define the image, task CPU/memory, networking and roles; Fargate supplies isolated task compute.
  • ECS still schedules tasks/services. You continue to own the container, IAM permissions, security groups and application behavior.
  • Task-local storage is ephemeral. Use supported EFS integration when tasks need shared persistent files.

Decision boundary. Fargate is container compute; ECS is orchestration. Fargate does not build images or define infrastructure templates. Choose self-managed EC2 capacity when host-level requirements demand it.

Capacity choiceTrade-off
FargateManaged task compute; supported CPU/memory/platform combinations
Fargate SpotDiscounted interruptible capacity; design interruption-tolerant work
ECS on EC2Host control and host-capacity responsibilities

Amazon RDS

Managed relational databases with SQL and transactions.

  • Read replicas asynchronously copy data; the application must send reads to replica endpoints. Expect possible replication lag.
  • A traditional Multi-AZ DB instance has a standby for failover, not reads.
  • A Multi-AZ DB cluster has readable standby DB instances; engine/configuration support matters.

Decision boundary. Read load points to replicas; failover points to Multi-AZ; repeated reusable results may point to a cache. These choices can coexist.

OptionMain purposeReadable secondary?
Read replicaScale readsYes; async replication lag
Multi-AZ DB instanceAvailability / failoverNo
Multi-AZ DB clusterAvailability + read capacityYes, supported cluster engines
SQL transactions, OLTP and OLAP

With RDS MySQL / InnoDB, wrap a voucher/game purchase in START TRANSACTION → debit / create entitlement with correct locking or conditions → COMMIT. On failure, ROLLBACK the transaction explicitly as appropriate; do not assume every SQL error aborts the entire transaction. Autocommit on separate statements does not make them one atomic bundle.

OLTP serves many short operational reads/writes (orders, balances); OLAP scans/aggregates historical datasets for analytics (for example a Redshift warehouse). SQL is used in both; a read replica scales reads but does not turn every OLTP schema into an analytics warehouse.

-- Conceptual MySQL/InnoDB transaction (application checks debit row count)
START TRANSACTION;
UPDATE players SET credits = credits - 10
WHERE id = 42 AND credits >= 10;
-- If no row changed: ROLLBACK; do not grant the entitlement.
INSERT INTO entitlements(player_id, game_id) VALUES (42, 7);
COMMIT;
-- Catch failure and ROLLBACK; use a unique purchase/request ID.
Automated backups vs long-term snapshots

RDS DB-instance automated-backup retention is 0–35 days (0 disables it); Multi-AZ DB clusters use 1–35 days. Creation defaults differ: CLI/API DB instance default 1 day, console default 7 days. Point-in-time recovery creates a new database resource.

Manual snapshots persist until explicitly deleted. For longer-term policy-based retention, use manual snapshots or an appropriate AWS Backup plan. Replicas and Multi-AZ are not a backup retention policy.

For a custom periodic DB-instance snapshot workflow: EventBridge Scheduler → Lambda → CreateDBSnapshot with execution permissions and unique names. Scheduler can also call supported AWS APIs directly; Lambda is useful when custom naming/retention logic is needed. Define cleanup, idempotency and snapshot-quota handling.

Exam trigger. Retain backups beyond the automated retention window → snapshots/AWS Backup, not an oversized BackupRetentionPeriod.

Route reads explicitly 
# Application routing, not an AWS API payload
write_connection = connect(primary_endpoint)
report_connection = connect(read_replica_endpoint)
# Use the primary for reads that require the latest committed value.
