Amazon ElastiCache

Keep frequently reused data in memory.

  • Valkey, Redis OSS and Memcached support low-latency cached access; choose engine capabilities deliberately.
  • A cache hit can reduce database work. A miss still needs a source-of-truth lookup.
  • Use expiry and invalidation to manage staleness. Memcached is not a durable primary database.

Decision boundary. A cache endpoint does not execute relational SQL in place of RDS. Cache-aside requires application logic and a key design.

DeploymentOperational choicePricing shape
ServerlessService manages cache capacityData storage + request/compute usage
Node-basedSelect node types/count/topologyProvisioned nodes; reservation options where supported
Try it · Shards vs replicas

One Region, node-based Redis OSS/Valkey cluster mode enabled. Each shard owns a different part of the keyspace.

Change the scenario

Three shards each have a primary and no replicas. Add shards for aggregate write/storage capacity; add replicas for reads and failover candidates.

Standard node-based cache with durability mode off. Illustrative stable hash and even slot ranges, not actual Redis CRC16 placement or a real resharding/failover procedure. Nodes can span AZs; async replicas are not guaranteed zero-data-loss copies. Local learning model; no AWS requests.

Try it · Lazy load, write-through or invalidate

Read first, write an updated value, then read again; compare the cache and database.

Change the example

Lazy+TTL: read $100, update DB to $120, then an unexpired cache can still return $100. TTL expiry does not refresh it; the next read fetches $120. Write-through updates; invalidation deletes.

One item, serial calls; changing item/strategy resets the example. Write-through/invalidation are shown synchronously, but can also be asynchronous. Separate DB/cache calls and concurrent readers need stronger controls for strict freshness. Local learning model; no AWS requests.

Redis/Valkey vs Memcached: replicas, failover and shards

Think of it as: Shards are different book collections; replicas are extra copies of the same collection. Extra copies let more people read, not write to a new collection.

Flow. Client hashes key → owning shard primary → asynchronous replica copy; read-capable clients can use replicas deliberately.

Read-heavy repeated database results and expensive computed values (rendered pages, recommendations, aggregations) can both benefit from caching. Key by the actual inputs and set invalidation/TTL; non-reusable CPU work is not accelerated merely by adding a cache.

This engine/topology comparison describes node-based clusters. ElastiCache Serverless manages availability across AZs itself; do not generalise node-based Memcached failure behaviour to its serverless offering. The standard cache-node topology below excludes the newer Valkey 9.0+ durability mode, which uses a Multi-AZ transactional log and has different write/recovery guarantees.

A node is one running cache server; a shard owns a subset of the keyspace; a node-based Redis replication group/cluster contains one or more shards. Cluster mode disabled has one shard; enabled supports multiple. Each shard has one primary and optional replicas. Redis Cluster maps keys to 16,384 hash slots.

Asynchronous replication copies each primary’s data to its replicas in both modes. Replicas increase read capacity and provide promotion candidates, not additional writers. Shards scale aggregate writes/storage. Enable automatic failover/Multi-AZ with an appropriate replica topology for availability; replication can lose recent writes during failure.

Both node-based Redis OSS/Valkey and Memcached clusters are regional; nodes can span AZs. More nodes is not cross-Region deployment. A hot single key still maps to one shard.

For the DynamoDB-native cache vs general-purpose cache vs CDN choice, use the DAX/Redis/CloudFront comparison.

Scroll the table horizontally on a narrow screen.

Engine/topologyCapabilityChoose with care
Redis OSS / ValkeyRich data types, replication and supported persistence/HA featuresReplication group: primary writes, replicas read; Multi-AZ automatic failover promotes a replica
Redis/Valkey cluster modeMultiple shards partition keyspace; each shard has its own primary and optional replicasSharding increases aggregate capacity; replicas/failover improve read/availability characteristics
Node-based MemcachedSimple multithreaded distributed cache; client distributes keys across nodesNo Redis-style replication groups, automatic replica promotion or durable primary storage

Exam trigger. Need replication + automatic failover or rich structures → supported Redis/Valkey topology. Need disposable simple distributed cache → Memcached can fit.

Common trap. A replica is not an extra write shard; a cache is not the relational SQL endpoint.

Cache strategy: who updates the cached representation?

Think of it as: Lazy loading fills a shelf when someone asks; TTL puts a use-by time on it; write-through replaces the shelf copy; invalidation removes the old copy.

  1. 1 · Read cache first
  2. 2 · Miss → database → populate
  3. 3 · Write → update or invalidate cache

These are application patterns, not a Redis setting that makes database/cache writes atomic. Write-through updates the cached representation; write-invalidate deletes it after the database commit. Either write workflow can be synchronous or asynchronous; latency, ordering, failures and races still need design.

Exam examples: popular profiles + limited cache + up to 60 s staleness → lazy loading + TTL; blog updates + fresher cached content → write-through is the intended pattern; product price updates without maintaining a cached representation → database write then invalidate. Strict zero-staleness needs stronger consistency/concurrency controls than these basic patterns alone.

Scroll the table horizontally on a narrow screen.

PatternRead / write behaviourTrade-off
Lazy loadingMiss fetches DB and populates cache; DB writes alone do not update cacheOnly requested items cached; can remain stale until eviction/invalidation
Lazy + TTLSame miss path; entries expire after a chosen durationNext read refreshes; expiry itself performs no DB fetch
Write-throughDB write + cache set/update in the application workflowFresher on successful writes; can cache never-read data and adds write work
Write-invalidateDB commit → delete cache key → next read repopulatesAvoids maintaining new cached value; failed delete/concurrent reads can still leave stale data

Exam trigger. Choose by freshness tolerance, read reuse and write workflow—not merely by engine name.

Common trap. A TTL does not refresh automatically. Updating the DB and cache in two calls is not an atomic transaction.

Cache-aside pseudocode 
key = f"game:{name}:{version}"
value = cache.get(key)
if value is None:
    value = database.load_game(name, version)
    cache.set(key, serialize(value), ttl=60)
return deserialize_if_needed(value)

AWS reference: Engine and deployment options · Engine comparison · Replication groups · Cluster mode and slots · Regional / AZ placement · Caching patterns

IAM, STS & Access Analyzer

Establish AWS trust and evaluate permissions.

  • Identity policies grant actions; supported resource policies grant access to resources. A role trust policy says who may assume it; STS issues temporary credentials.
  • Permissions boundaries and SCPs limit applicable permissions; they do not grant actions. An explicit applicable deny overrides an allow.
  • Access Analyzer finds supported external/unused access and validates policies. Policy variables can scope reusable access, e.g. an IAM user’s own S3 prefix.

Decision boundary. Trusting an identity does not authorize every resource. ${aws:username} is for IAM users and is not generally present for role sessions; use suitable principal tags/identity variables.

Try it · IAM identity vs queue policy

Evaluate one IAM principal and one SQS action, in the same account or across accounts.

Change the scenario

Same account: either applicable Allow can suffice. Cross-account IAM access: both sides typically allow. Applicable explicit Deny always wins.

Only policies matching this principal, action, resource and conditions are toggled. Other controls are assumed satisfied: SCPs/RCPs, boundaries, session/endpoint policies and KMS can restrict access. SNS service-principal evaluation is a separate example, not modelled as an IAM role. Local learning model; no AWS requests.

Try it · EC2 credentials vs S3 bucket access

Detach the role and expire its cached credentials separately; inspect GetObject and PutObject.

Change the example

Detachment stops ongoing credential supply after propagation, not every already-issued credential. A separate public bucket read grant can still allow GetObject; an explicit PutObject Deny wins.

Existing role remains defined with the selected policies; it is detached, not deleted. Public read is a hypothetical independently allowed path, not a recommendation. Named-principal bucket grants need valid matching credentials. Other IAM/BPA/network controls are assumed satisfied; no five-minute grace is modelled. Objects in this access-only model have no extra KMS decryption requirement. Local learning model; no AWS requests.

Identity policy vs SQS queue policy

Think of it as: An identity policy is an employee’s badge; a queue policy is the guest list on the room. A role trust policy controls who can borrow a badge.

Flow. Lambda uses its execution role → sqs:SendMessage → SQS evaluates applicable identity/queue policies. There is no special “SQS role”.

Scroll the table horizontally on a narrow screen.

PolicyAttached to / questionExample
Identity-basedIAM user/group/role: what may this identity do?Lambda execution role allows sqs:SendMessage on Orders
Resource-basedSQS queue: which Principal may do what here?Queue allows sns.amazonaws.com to send, restricted by aws:SourceArn
Cross-account IAM accessTypically requires both identity-side and queue-side AllowsAccount A role → account B queue
Role trustIAM role: who may assume this role?sts:AssumeRole; not a queue permission
 
// Queue policy statement: SNS → one queue (JSON excerpt)
{"Effect":"Allow","Principal":{"Service":"sns.amazonaws.com"},
 "Action":"sqs:SendMessage",
 "Resource":"arn:aws:sqs:ap-southeast-2:222222222222:Orders",
 "Condition":{"ArnEquals":{"aws:SourceArn":
   "arn:aws:sns:ap-southeast-2:222222222222:OrderEvents"}}}

Exam trigger. Allow SNS to deliver to SQS → queue resource policy with the SNS service Principal and source restriction.

Common trap. Same-account policies often combine as a union; applicable explicit Deny wins. SCPs/RCPs, boundaries, sessions, endpoint policies, principal type and KMS permissions can further change the result.

Decode an encoded authorisation failure

Think of it as: Open a sealed diagnostic report with the authorised decoder; it does not unlock the denied door.

Flow. Failed AWS API → encoded message → authorised STS decode call → inspect explicit/implicit denial.

Some AWS access-denied responses include encoded diagnostic details. STS decodes them; the caller needs sts:DecodeAuthorizationMessage, not necessarily administrator access. Decoding reveals context; it does not grant the failed operation.

# AWS CLI; substitute the encoded message from the error
aws sts decode-authorization-message \
  --encoded-message 'ENCODED_MESSAGE' \
  --query DecodedMessage --output text

Exam trigger. Encoded authorisation failure → sts decode-authorization-message.

Common trap. Neither IAM nor KMS provides this CLI operation; not every access-denied error contains an encoded message.

EC2 role removal vs S3 bucket permissions

Think of it as: Taking away the badge dispenser does not instantly invalidate every badge already issued, and the room may have its own guest/public access rules.

  1. 1 · EC2 credentials / anonymous request
  2. 2 · Identity + bucket policies
  3. 3 · Applicable limits / Deny
  4. 4 · GetObject or PutObject decision

EC2 obtains temporary credentials through its instance profile. Detaching/removing the role stops that ongoing source once the change propagates; previously issued credentials can remain usable until expiry unless permissions are revoked/denied. Removing a role from a profile can have propagation delay; do not use it as an immediate revocation mechanism.

Every S3 request evaluates its actual credentials and applicable policies. A bucket policy can grant a named principal access, or public/anonymous access when Block Public Access and other controls permit it. A named-principal grant still needs the right authenticated principal. There is no special five-minute S3 read grace period; a surviving credential or independent resource grant explains continued access.

Exam trigger. Reads continue after role detachment → identify the credentials and bucket policy used, not a fictional S3 grace timer.

Common trap. Detaching a role is different from deleting it or revoking its sessions. An applicable explicit Deny wins; SCPs/RCPs, boundaries, sessions, endpoints and BPA still matter.

IAM-user prefix policy (illustrative) 
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [{
    "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "s3:GetObject",
    "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::study-home/${aws:username}/*"
  }]
}

Billing-console access can require the account root user to Activate IAM Access plus appropriate IAM permissions. SCPs govern member-account principals within their documented scope; they are not a universal policy attached to every possible caller.

AWS reference: Policy evaluation · Access Analyzer · Policy variables · Billing console activation · SQS evaluation · STS diagnostic decoder · Instance profiles / propagation · Revoke role sessions

Security groups, NACLs & VPC endpoints

Filter network traffic at two different boundaries.

  • Security groups attach to network interfaces and are stateful: allowed traffic automatically permits its response.
  • NACLs operate at subnet boundaries and are stateless: allow the required request and return traffic, including ephemeral ports.
  • Check routes, security groups, NACLs, listener and target health separately when diagnosing connectivity.

Decision boundary. Network reachability does not authenticate a user or grant an IAM action. Security groups use allow rules only; NACLs support allow and deny.

ControlScopeRulesResponse traffic
Security groupNetwork interfaceAllow onlyStateful
NACLSubnet boundaryAllow + deny; rule orderStateless; explicit return rules
Try it · Stateful SG vs stateless NACL

Model one TCP connection at the receiving subnet. The frontend and backend are separate connections.

Change the scenario

Browser:54321 → ALB:80; ALB:80 → Browser:54321. Stateful SG permits the response; stateless NACL needs an outbound destination-port rule for 54321.

Initiator-side controls/routes and target application are assumed permitted. This is ordinary tracked TCP traffic; special untracked flows are outside the exercise. Actual ephemeral ranges depend on the initiator. Local learning model; no AWS requests.

Try it · Private-subnet service access

Assume EC2 has no public IP, NAT or IGW path; choose the endpoint mechanism and its configuration.

Change the example

EC2 → S3/DynamoDB gateway endpoint uses a service-prefix-list route, not an endpoint ENI. Secrets Manager/KMS use supported interface endpoints with private ENIs and security groups.

Same-Region standard connectivity; EC2 egress SG, NACLs, normal local routing, IAM/resource/endpoint policies are assumed permitted. S3 and DynamoDB also support interface endpoints. The service itself remains regional, outside the customer subnet. Local learning model; no AWS requests.

Follow the destination port in each direction

Think of it as: A stateful guard remembers your visit and lets you leave; a stateless checkpoint checks the outbound ticket again.

Flow. Browser:54321 → ALB:80 → response to :54321; independently ALB:40000 → EC2:80 → response to :40000.

A browser chooses an ephemeral source port: Browser:54321 → ALB:80; the response is ALB:80 → Browser:54321. HTTPS normally uses destination 443. SG connection tracking permits the response; a stateless NACL needs its own return rule.

ALB creates a separate backend connection, for example ALB:40000 → EC2:80. The browser’s 54321 is not reused as the backend destination. Actual ephemeral ranges depend on the initiating OS/service; 1024–65535 is commonly used in ELB-related NACL configurations.

Scroll the table horizontally on a narrow screen.

Subnet / legInbound NACL destinationOutbound NACL destination
ALB subnet: browser connection80 or 443 from allowed clientsClient ephemeral range
ALB subnet: backend connectionALB ephemeral range from backendBackend application/health-check ports
EC2 subnet: backend connectionBackend application/health-check ports from ALBALB ephemeral range

Exam trigger. Request arrives but reply times out → inspect return routes and outbound/inbound ephemeral-port NACL rules.

Common trap. Security groups have allow rules only; NACLs have ordered allow/deny rules. Opening only 80/443 in both NACL directions misses the return destination port.

Gateway vs interface endpoints: route entry vs private ENI

Think of it as: A gateway endpoint changes the road sign in the route table; an interface endpoint builds a private service entrance at a local IP.

Gateway endpoints support S3 and DynamoDB, use service-prefix-list route-table entries, and create no endpoint ENI or endpoint security group. Normal public service DNS/IP addressing can still use that private AWS-network route; no NAT/IGW is required.

Interface endpoints use AWS PrivateLink with private-IP ENIs in selected subnets/AZs, endpoint security groups and eligible private/endpoint DNS. They are regional resources and usually incur hourly/data-processing charges. S3 and DynamoDB both support gateway and interface endpoints; a gateway is commonly simplest for ordinary same-VPC access. Interface endpoints address additional connectivity cases, including supported on-premises access.

Scroll the table horizontally on a narrow screen.

BoundaryGateway endpointInterface endpoint
MechanismPrefix-list route-table targetPrivateLink + endpoint ENIs/private IPs
Supported examplesS3 and DynamoDBSecrets Manager, KMS, S3, DynamoDB and many more
Security group on endpointNoneYes; typically allow required HTTPS source/port
DNSNormal public service endpoint can use private routePrivate DNS or endpoint-specific hostname selects ENIs
Charging / placementNo additional endpoint charge; route-table associationUsually hourly + data; regional endpoint, ENIs in chosen AZs

Exam trigger. Private EC2 → S3/DynamoDB without NAT and minimal endpoint cost → gateway. Private-IP entry to KMS/Secrets Manager → interface.

Common trap. Private connectivity is not IAM authorisation. Do not claim DynamoDB supports gateway endpoints only, or place the regional service itself inside your subnet.

Request path to inspect 
client --HTTPS 443--> public ALB
ALB security group --app port--> private target security group
subnet NACL: allow request + return-port traffic both ways

Amazon S3

Store objects; separate access, browser sharing, replication and encryption.

  • New S3 uploads are encrypted by default. SSE-S3 uses AES256; SSE-KMS uses aws:kms in the encryption request header.
  • Default bucket encryption chooses storage encryption even when the client omits a header.
  • A bucket policy can require an explicit mode/key. Missing-header checks and incorrect-value checks express different requirements.

Decision boundary. Requiring a request header rejects clients that rely on bucket defaults. Requiring aws:kms alone does not pin a particular KMS key; validate its key ID/ARN when required.

Compare S3 encryption responsibilities

Logging and CORS: storage access vs browser permission

Use source bucket → separate logging bucket, in the same account and Region. Logging deliveries to the source bucket generate further requests and recursive log growth; leave destination-bucket server access logging off.

CORS is configured on the resource server (S3), enforced by the browser. The browser sends Origin; an allowed response contains Access-Control-Allow-Origin. A preflight also checks allowed methods/headers. Server-to-server clients do not enforce browser CORS.

Bucket/IAM policies decide whether the operation is authorised. CORS only permits a browser to expose an otherwise permitted cross-origin response; it does not grant S3 access.

GET /manual.pdf HTTP/1.1
Origin: https://app.smart.com

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.smart.com
# Illustrative headers; S3 CORS rules control the response.

Exam trigger. Browser code at app.smart.com reads an S3 resource: configure CORS on that S3 bucket and independently allow the object operation.

Common trap. Changing browser code or adding an allow bucket policy alone does not supply the resource server’s CORS response.

Replication, existing objects, metadata and lifecycle

SRR stays in one Region; CRR copies to another Region. Live rules apply to eligible new objects after configuration; versioning and the replication role are required. Use S3 Batch Replication for eligible pre-existing objects or missed replicas.

Object user metadata and tags can replicate with objects; tag-based rule selection requires the matching tags on the original upload. Later-tagged existing objects can need Batch Replication. Configure permissions and replica-modification behaviour for your case.

Lifecycle actions are not replicated. Set lifecycle rules independently on the destination. Do not infer that expiring the source object also expires its replica; delete-marker replication is a separate configurable feature with exceptions.

Exam trigger. Backfill existing data after creating a replication rule → Batch Replication, not just wait for the live rule.

Access controls, signed URLs and AWS partitions

Identity policies grant a principal actions; bucket policies grant/deny resource access. Legacy ACLs grant limited object/bucket access, but Bucket owner enforced Object Ownership disables ACLs by default. Prefer policies.

A presigned S3 URL delegates an operation using the signer’s credentials and permissions, for a bounded validity period; it does not bypass explicit denies, expired credentials or KMS checks. A permissions boundary caps applicable identity permissions without granting them.

An ARN partition (aws, aws-cn, aws-us-gov) is an isolated AWS identity/service boundary, not a folder. An S3 prefix such as customers/alice/ is part of an object key. Standard IAM role delegation/resource-policy grants do not bridge partitions; use separately authorised data-transfer designs where permitted.

CloudFront signed URLs differ from S3 presigning: the application signs with a private key and CloudFront verifies a public key in a trusted key group (recommended). Legacy CloudFront account key pairs use the account root user; normal IAM access keys are not CloudFront signing keys.

Common trap. A valid URL signature proves the configured signing contract, not ownership of arbitrary objects or cross-partition IAM trust.

SSE-C, client-side encryption and HTTPS

Think of it as: SSE-C lends the warehouse your key to lock the box; client-side encryption delivers an already locked box.

Flow. SSE-C: client + key over TLS → S3 encrypts → encrypted object; client-side: client encrypts → S3 stores ciphertext.

SSE-C sends the customer-provided key with each relevant request over HTTPS; S3 performs encryption/decryption and does not persist that key. S3 rejects SSE-C over HTTP. Client-side encryption encrypts before upload, so S3 receives ciphertext. See the existing encryption comparison. The customer sends an actual SSE-C key, not a KMS key ARN. SSE-C does not require KMS; importing key material into KMS is a separate concept. Try the key-flow selector beside the existing comparison.

Enforce HTTPS for all relevant S3 requests with an explicit bucket-policy Deny on aws:SecureTransport=false. Other encryption modes do not inherently impose that same SSE-C-specific request requirement. Account for AWS-service-to-service access using the documented principal conditions where appropriate.

// Bucket-policy statement excerpt: deny HTTP for this bucket and objects
{"Effect":"Deny","Principal":"*","Action":"s3:*",
 "Resource":["arn:aws:s3:::study-bucket","arn:aws:s3:::study-bucket/*"],
 "Condition":{"Bool":{"aws:SecureTransport":"false"}}}

Exam trigger. S3-managed keys → SSE-S3; KMS-protected data keys/key control → SSE-KMS; actual customer key supplied to S3 → SSE-C.

Common trap. SSE-C is still server-side encryption. TLS protects transit; it does not replace encryption at rest. New SSE-C defaults may block its use unless explicitly permitted.

CLI pagination: service pages vs output pages

Think of it as: The warehouse sends boxes to the clerk (service pages); the clerk gives you a limited pile and a claim ticket (CLI output page).

  1. 1 · S3 ListObjectsV2 service calls
  2. 2 · CLI limits output
  3. 3 · NextToken → --starting-token

The shared CLI playground includes S3 objects (250): –max-items 100 produces output pages of 100 → 100 → 50. –page-size controls underlying API call batching, not the total output limit. Pass the CLI NextToken unchanged to –starting-token; do not substitute a raw S3 continuation token or invent a generic –next-token option.

# Executable AWS CLI shape
aws s3api list-objects-v2 --bucket my-bucket --max-items 100
# Next output page (omit --starting-token on the first call):
aws s3api list-objects-v2 --bucket my-bucket --max-items 100 \
  --starting-token "TOKEN_FROM_PREVIOUS_RESPONSE"

Exam trigger. Limit CLI output → --max-items; resume → --starting-token. Smaller internal service calls → --page-size.

Common trap. Tokens are opaque and command-specific. Reuse the same relevant command settings; CLI tokens differ from service API cursors.

Explicit SSE-KMS header enforcement policy 
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [{
    "Sid": "DenyMissingEncryptionHeader",
    "Effect": "Deny", "Principal": "*",
    "Action": "s3:PutObject", "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::study-bucket/*",
    "Condition": {"Null": {"s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption": "true"}}
  }, {
    "Sid": "DenyWrongEncryptionMode",
    "Effect": "Deny", "Principal": "*",
    "Action": "s3:PutObject", "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::study-bucket/*",
    "Condition": {"StringNotEquals": {"s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption": "aws:kms"}}
  }]
}

Illustrative bucket name. This narrow policy shows request enforcement, not complete bucket access. KMS upload/download permissions and bucket policies must also allow the intended principal.

AWS reference: SSE-KMS and enforcement · Server logging · CORS · What replication copies · Batch Replication · Access controls · Partitions · CloudFront signers · SSE-C requirements · Transport policy conditions · CLI ListObjectsV2

AWS KMS

Control cryptographic keys and cryptographic operations.

  • For symmetric encryption KMS keys, Encrypt accepts up to 4,096 bytes. Use envelope encryption for large application data; KMS protects the data key, not the 111 GB file directly.
  • GenerateDataKey returns plaintext and encrypted copies of a data key. Encrypt data locally, discard plaintext key, store the encrypted key with ciphertext.
  • Normal crypto calls do not return the underlying KMS key material. Rotation support depends on key type/origin; rotating key material is not recreating a key per request.

Decision boundary. Encryption does not replace authorization. A principal needs the relevant service access and KMS key-use authorization; cross-account use requires compatible policies.

Compare cryptography patterns and KMS example calls

Choose the API by the returned material

Encrypt returns ciphertext; Decrypt returns recovered plaintext. GenerateDataKey returns a plaintext data key AND its encrypted representation. GenerateDataKeyWithoutPlaintext returns only the encrypted data key. GenerateDataKeyWithPlaintext is not an API.

The KMS key stays under KMS protection. The application stores ciphertext, encrypted data key and encryption metadata; discard plaintext data-key material after use. KMS does not retain both returned copies as application storage. Eligible, deliberately configured SDK caching is a bounded exception to immediate data-key disposal; compare the caching section below.

Exam trigger. Large-file encryption with a separately controlled key → envelope encryption; compare the two-client flow in the cryptography section.

Bounded data-key caching: fewer KMS calls, more retained material

Think of it as: Briefly retain a protected work key for a bounded batch; it is not permission to reuse the same seal/nonce or keep the key indefinitely.

  1. 1 · Eligible cache lookup
  2. 2 · Reuse within thresholds, or KMS call
  3. 3 · Encrypt with correct fresh message material

The AWS Encryption SDK can reuse eligible cached cryptographic materials, reducing KMS requests, latency, cost and throttling. Cache age, message-count and encrypted-byte thresholds bound reuse; matching algorithm/context and SDK support matter. Protect cached plaintext material and use the minimum reuse needed.

A fresh key per encryption is the normal default. Data-key reuse never permits IV/nonce reuse; follow the SDK’s supported algorithms and metadata handling. Backoff/jitter and quota planning also address KMS throttling. S3 Bucket Keys optimise S3 SSE-KMS, not arbitrary application transaction encryption. See the request counter in the cryptography comparison.

Exam trigger. Many eligible application encryptions bottlenecked on KMS requests → evaluate bounded SDK caching and retries, with security thresholds.

Common trap. The simple request counter is not an exact caching-CMM implementation. Supported SDK/keyring alternatives differ; KMS itself is not storing your application’s plaintext data-key cache.

Large-payload encryption pseudocode 
# Envelope encryption, conceptual flow
plain_key, encrypted_key = kms.generate_data_key(key_id, key_spec="AES_256")
ciphertext = authenticated_encrypt(plain_key, document)
securely_discard(plain_key)
store(ciphertext, encrypted_key)
# Later: KMS Decrypt(encrypted_key) → data key → decrypt document.

AWS reference: Envelope encryption · Data keys · Key rotation · Encrypt limits · GenerateDataKey · WithoutPlaintext · SDK data-key caching · Caching thresholds

Amazon Cognito

Authenticate application users; federate them into AWS access when needed.

  • User pools provide a user directory/federation and issue ID/access JWTs plus refresh tokens.
  • Identity pools exchange supported identities for temporary AWS credentials, including narrowly scoped guest access when enabled.
  • API Gateway can authorize with Cognito tokens; a Lambda authorizer supports custom token validation/rules. HTTP APIs have native JWT authorizers.

Decision boundary. A user-pool JWT is not an access key. A browser may call your API with a bearer token, while the backend calls AWS with its own role credentials.

RequirementChooseWhat comes out
Sign in app usersUser pool (+ external IdP if needed)ID/access JWT + refresh token
Direct AWS resource accessIdentity pool + IAM roleTemporary access key/secret/session token
Custom API rulesLambda authorizerAPI authorization result
AWS API invocationAuthorized IAM principal + SigV4Signed request
Different credential contracts 
# Authenticated application → protected API
Authorization: Bearer <access-token-JWT>

# Direct AWS SDK access uses temporary credentials instead
{"AccessKeyId":"<temporary-id>",
 "SecretKey":"<temporary-secret>",
 "SessionToken":"<session-token>",
 "Expiration":"<expiry>"}

Validate token signature, issuer, audience/client binding, token_use and expiry; apply required scopes and record/tenant rules. User and identity pools can be combined. Never place a secret credential in a public client bundle.

AWS reference: User pools · Identity pools and AWS credentials · API authorizer choices

Secrets Manager & Parameter Store

Separate credentials from application configuration.

  • Secrets Manager stores secrets and supports automatic rotation through service-managed integrations or Lambda workflows, depending on secret type.
  • Parameter Store stores named configuration, versions and encrypted SecureString values; it has no equivalent native database-password rotation workflow.
  • Grant runtime roles narrow read/decrypt access. Retrieve and cache values appropriately; do not embed secrets in code or logs.

Decision boundary. Rotating RDS credentials points to Secrets Manager. An expiration notification/parameter policy is not a password-rotation implementation.

OptionUsePricing / lifecycle
Secrets ManagerCredentials + rotationPer secret + API use; integration-specific rotation
Parameter Store StandardSmall static configStandard storage free; throughput options may bill
Parameter Store AdvancedLarger values, policies, more scalePer advanced parameter + API/throughput charges
AppConfigValidated configuration / feature rolloutSeparate controlled deployment capability
Runtime retrieval commands 
# AWS CLI; never print this result in application logs
aws secretsmanager get-secret-value --secret-id prod/orders/db
aws ssm get-parameter --name /prod/orders/endpoint
aws ssm get-parameter --name /prod/orders/token --with-decryption

SecureString needs appropriate KMS permissions. Parameter Store can reference a Secrets Manager secret as a pass-through; the rotation capability still belongs to Secrets Manager.

AWS reference: Parameter Store comparison · Secrets rotation

CloudWatch, CloudTrail & tracing

Choose evidence that can actually answer the question.

  • CloudWatch metrics show aggregate demand/latency/errors; Logs hold application events when configured.
  • ALB access logs show client IP, path, timing and status. CloudTrail shows supported AWS API/account events, not every HTTP request.
  • Trace IDs correlate requests; distributed tracing reveals downstream latency when the application/services are instrumented.

Decision boundary. Check target health settings and reachability before scaling an unhealthy target. Adding capacity does not fix a wrong health-check path or denied request.

Try it · Choose the metric source

First identify the signal; then decide whether you need a new publisher or simply faster native samples.

Change the scenario

CPU → native metric. Memory → agent/custom publisher. App-specific rate → instrumentation. ALB requests/target → ALB native metric if an ALB exists. Faster EC2 native samples → detailed monitoring.

A valid metric must exist with the correct dimensions and scaling behaviour. Standard custom resolution is 60 s; high-resolution custom data uses StorageResolution=1. Detailed EC2 monitoring is normally 1 minute, not 1 second. Local learning model; no AWS requests.

Try it · X-Ray annotation vs metadata

Enrich one sampled trace, search its indexed annotation, then try searching metadata.

Change the example

Annotations are indexed scalar labels; metadata can hold nested debugging data but is not an indexed X-Ray filter. DynamoDB appears through an instrumented client subsegment/inferred node.

Deterministic illustrative batch of 20 requests; generate a new batch to apply the chosen sampling rate. This is not the default reservoir algorithm. No real traces are emitted; avoid putting sensitive values in telemetry. Local learning model; no AWS requests.

Custom signals, metric filters and error rates

Standard custom metric resolution is 60 seconds; high-resolution custom metrics use StorageResolution=1 for one-second data. Resolution is distinct from which metric you publish.

A metric filter turns matching incoming log events into numerical metrics for graphs/alarms; it is not retroactive. Logs Insights queries logs for investigation/aggregation; a query alone is not a continuously emitted custom metric.

For an external API, instrument your application’s calls: emit total requests and failed requests (consistent dimensions/periods and a defined failure rule), then metric math IF(total > 0, 100 × failures / total, 0). Alarm on sustained error percentage → SNS notification. NetworkOut or a count of all app errors does not measure that API’s failure ratio. Treat missing telemetry separately from zero traffic; configure alarm missing-data behaviour deliberately.

// PutMetricData excerpt: both counters share namespace/dimensions
{"Namespace":"Study/Payments","MetricData":[
 {"MetricName":"Requests","Value":100,"Unit":"Count","StorageResolution":1},
 {"MetricName":"Failures","Value":4,"Unit":"Count","StorageResolution":1}
]}
// Sum over the same period: error_pct = 100 * 4 / 100 = 4%

Exam trigger. Need a third-party API error rate → publish/count both failures and total calls; use metric math and an alarm.

X-Ray: traces, annotations, metadata and sampling

Think of it as: A trace is the delivery journey; segments are each depot’s work; annotations are indexed labels; metadata is the detailed note inside the parcel.

  1. 1 · API Gateway segment
  2. 2 · Lambda segment
  3. 3 · DynamoDB client subsegment / inferred node

The default X-Ray sampling rule uses a 1 request/second reservoir plus 5% of additional requests. Central reservoir quotas are shared; local fallback rules can sample independently per process. Upstream sampling decisions and service-specific behaviour also matter.

A matching custom rule with a fixed rate of 1.0 can request 100% sampling for debugging. Ensure the upstream/root service samples and downstream instrumentation propagates context; instrumentation gaps, quotas and unsupported paths can still prevent a complete trace.

CloudWatch metrics answer “how much/how often”; logs record application events; X-Ray traces instrumented request paths; CloudTrail records supported AWS API/account activity. Prefer OpenTelemetry/ADOT for new instrumentation: X-Ray SDKs/daemon entered maintenance in February 2026.

Scroll the table horizontally on a narrow screen.

ConceptPurposeBoundary
TraceEnd-to-end request journeyGroups related segments by trace ID
SegmentWork performed by an instrumented serviceNot a CloudFormation/infrastructure stack
SubsegmentDownstream operation or finer workAn instrumented Lambda → DynamoDB call produces a client subsegment; DynamoDB does not emit its own X-Ray segment
AnnotationIndexed searchable scalar key/valueString, number or Boolean; use trace filter expressions
MetadataNon-indexed debugging detailCan contain nested objects/arrays; application/instrumentation adds it deliberately, not necessarily automatically
SamplingChoose which requests are tracedLimits telemetry volume/overhead; no trace exists for an unsampled request

Exam trigger. Search traces by business tag → annotation. Store structured debug context → metadata, then inspect a selected trace.

Common trap. Metadata is not an indexed filter field or a relational column. The downstream DynamoDB node is inferred from client instrumentation.

Metric source vs collection frequency

Think of it as: A faster speedometer still does not measure fuel level; a different sensor is needed.

Flow. Actual signal → native/agent/application publisher → CloudWatch metric → alarm/scaling policy → ASG desired target.

Supported AWS services publish built-in metrics automatically. EC2 basic monitoring typically publishes native metrics every 5 minutes; detailed monitoring changes those metrics to 1 minute, not new guest-memory or filesystem measurements.

The CloudWatch Agent publishes guest metrics as custom metrics. Application-specific metrics have no predefined universal list: instrument them with PutMetricData, log metric filters or another publisher. A CloudWatch alarm can invoke an ASG scaling policy; the policy changes desired capacity and the ASG reconciles actual instances.

Scroll the table horizontally on a narrow screen.

MetricTypical source
EC2 CPU utilisationBuilt-in CPUUtilization
EC2 NetworkIn / NetworkOutBuilt-in
EC2 disk I/OBuilt-in where supported (EC2 instance-store metrics; EBS has its own volume metrics)
EC2 memory utilisationCloudWatch Agent / custom publisher
EC2 disk space percentageCloudWatch Agent / custom publisher
Application requests/minuteApplication instrumentation / log metric filter
Self-managed MySQL query rateCustom instrumentation
ALB RequestCountALB built-in, if an ALB exists
ALB RequestCountPerTargetALB built-in, if an ALB/target group exists

Exam trigger. One-minute native EC2 samples → detailed monitoring. Memory/disk space → agent/custom publishing. App-specific query rate → instrumentation.

Common trap. Detailed monitoring changes frequency, not metric inventory. No ALB in the architecture means no ALB request metric to scale from.

Investigation sequence 
symptom: HTTP 5xx increased after deployment
1. CloudWatch: when, how many, ALB or target errors?
2. ALB access logs: which path / target / status / timing?
3. Trace + app log: which dependency failed?
4. CloudTrail: who changed the configuration?

CloudTrail data events are service/operation-specific and often require explicit enablement. They do not replace application access logs. Avoid sensitive credentials/payloads in diagnostic logs.

AWS reference: ALB request evidence · CloudTrail event types · CloudWatch concepts · Log metric filters · Logs Insights · Metric math · X-Ray sampling · X-Ray SDK lifecycle · EC2 native metric definitions · EC2 detailed monitoring · Agent metrics · X-Ray concepts

AWS CodePipeline

Coordinate the stages that turn a source revision into a release.

  • Source, build/test, approval and deploy actions form an orchestrated delivery workflow.
  • CodePipeline passes artifacts and invokes action providers. CodeBuild runs build commands; CloudFormation and CodeDeploy perform their respective deployment actions.
  • A pipeline service role and action-specific permissions authorize delivery. They are separate from the runtime application role.

Decision boundary. A successful pipeline action proves that action succeeded; verify which artifact, configuration and route are actually serving production.

TypeChoiceCost comparison
V1Standard pipeline/stage/action structureCompare active-pipeline pricing
V2Adds release-safety and trigger configurationCompare action-execution pricing; see current rates
CI/CD roles and the retired CodeStar dashboard

Think of it as: CodePipeline is the conductor; CodeBuild makes/tests the instrument; CodeDeploy takes the release to the stage. CodeStar was the old project control room.

  1. 1 · Source via CodeConnections
  2. 2 · CodePipeline stages
  3. 3 · CodeBuild / CodeDeploy actions

Historical exam note: original AWS CodeStar project creation/dashboard capabilities were retired in July 2024. An old practice question about one unified development-project dashboard may intend CodeStar; do not treat that as a current onboarding recommendation.

AWS CodeConnections, formerly CodeStar Connections, is a separate repository-connection capability. Its former name does not mean it was retired with CodeStar projects. Modern pipelines connect a source provider, build/test artifacts, then deploy to the target.

Scroll the table horizontally on a narrow screen.

ServiceResponsibilityCurrent vs historical
CodeBuildBuild and testBuild artifacts, run commands/tests
CodeDeployApplication rolloutPlatform-specific deployment and lifecycle
CodePipelineOrchestrate CI/CD stages/actionsCoordinates source/build/deploy and approvals
CodeStarUnified project setup/dashboardOriginal capability retired July 2024
CodeConnectionsConnect supported external source providersSeparate capability, formerly CodeStar Connections

Exam trigger. Build/test → CodeBuild; deploy → CodeDeploy; coordinate stages → CodePipeline. Unified CodeStar projects → historical question.

Common trap. CodeStar and CodeStar Connections/CodeConnections are different service capabilities.

Pipeline build-stage excerpt 
{
  "name": "BuildAndTest",
  "actions": [{
    "name": "Build",
    "actionTypeId": {
      "category": "Build", "owner": "AWS",
      "provider": "CodeBuild", "version": "1"
    },
    "configuration": {"ProjectName": "orders-build"},
    "inputArtifacts": [{"name": "SourceOutput"}],
    "outputArtifacts": [{"name": "BuildOutput"}]
  }]
}

This is one stage, not a complete CreatePipeline request. Source connection, roles, artifact storage and deploy actions are configured elsewhere.

AWS reference: Pipeline responsibility · Pipeline types · Current pricing · Retired services · CodeConnections rename

AWS CodeBuild

Run build/test commands and produce a deployable artifact.

  • The buildspec defines phases, commands and artifact output. A managed build environment runs those commands.
  • Package Lambda ZIPs or container images for the target runtime. S3 stores build artifacts; ECR stores container images; CodeArtifact stores software packages.
  • Run unit/integration tests and inspect their results. Amazon Q Developer can assist with code and tests; developers still review and validate the result.

Decision boundary. Compiling code is not deploying it. A passing unit test does not prove the production integration, IAM permissions or active route are correct.

Compute choiceStarting clueWatch
EC2 on-demandFlexible build environment without a standing fleetImage, architecture and resource requirements
EC2 reserved capacityManage a fleet for predictable build demandCapacity commitment and utilization
Lambda computeFast startup for supported buildsSupported runtimes, features and duration limits
buildspec.yml for an illustrative Python project 
version: 0.2
phases:
  install:
    commands:
      - pip install -r requirements.txt -t package/
  build:
    commands:
      - python -m pytest tests/
      - cp app.py package/
      - cd package && zip -r ../function.zip .
artifacts:
  files:
    - function.zip

The example assumes a suitable Linux build image with pytest and zip available, and the named project files. Pin dependencies and select compute from measured build requirements.

AWS reference: CodeBuild role · Compute modes · Buildspec contract · Q Developer in exam scope

AWS CodeDeploy

Roll out an application revision using a platform-specific deployment contract.

  • Supports EC2/on-premises, Lambda and ECS deployment platforms.
  • The AppSpec describes target resources and lifecycle hooks. Deployment configuration controls rollout; configured alarms/hooks support validation and recovery.
  • Lambda traffic shifting moves an alias between published versions. ECS blue/green shifts service traffic; EC2 deployments can update in place or use replacements.

Decision boundary. CloudFormation manages declared resources and can deploy application resources/code. CodeDeploy specializes in rollout, hooks and traffic shifting; it does not build the artifact.

TargetRelease unitKey distinction
LambdaPublished versions + aliasCanary/linear/all-at-once traffic configuration
ECSTask definition + target serviceBlue/green task sets and traffic routing
EC2/on-premisesApplication revision + hooksIn-place or supported blue/green deployment
EC2 in-place lifecycle: stop, download, prepare, install, start, test

Think of it as: Stop the old app → download the update → prepare the room → install → finish setup → start → test.

Flow. ApplicationStop → DownloadBundle → BeforeInstall → Install → AfterInstall → ApplicationStart → ValidateService.

In-place updates application files on existing instances; it does not inherently replace EC2. Blue/green deploys to a replacement environment and shifts traffic, keeping the original environment for a controlled transition.

ApplicationStop uses scripts from the previous successful deployment’s AppSpec; it is skipped on the first deployment when none exists. DownloadBundle and Install are agent-reserved events, not custom-script hook locations. A load-balanced deployment can also have traffic-block/allow lifecycle events.

Scroll the table horizontally on a narrow screen.

Order / eventResponsibility
1 ApplicationStopStop previous application (previous successful revision)
2 DownloadBundleAgent downloads new revision
3 BeforeInstallCustom preparation
4 InstallAgent installs revision files
5 AfterInstallCustom configuration
6 ApplicationStartStart application
7 ValidateServiceVerify it works

Exam trigger. Prepare before new files are installed → BeforeInstall; downloading is the separate DownloadBundle event.

Common trap. Do not put DownloadBundle/Install under custom hooks. In-place lifecycle events are not Lambda alias lifecycle events.

Lambda AppSpec excerpt 
version: 0.0
Resources:
  - OrdersFunction:
      Type: AWS::Lambda::Function
      Properties:
        Name: orders
        Alias: prod
        CurrentVersion: '1'
        TargetVersion: '2'

The deployment group, service role, traffic policy, alarms and optional hooks are configured separately. Verify the actual alias/target and business health before considering a release complete.

AWS reference: Platforms and rollout · AppSpec examples · Lifecycle events and hooks

EventBridge & SNS

Route events or fan a publication out to independent consumers.

  • EventBridge connects event sources to matching targets; bus and feature selection determine supported routing/replay behavior.
  • SNS publishes to topics and pushes to subscribed endpoints. An SNS-to-SQS fanout gives consumers independent queues.
  • A consumer needs its own authorization, retry and idempotency handling. An accepted publication does not prove the business work completed.

Decision boundary. A router or topic does not retain the progress of a multi-step business workflow. A queue buffers pending work; a state machine coordinates steps.

NeedStarting choice
Route by event content / sourceEventBridge bus and matching target configuration
Publish once to multiple subscribersSNS topic; optional subscription filters
Independent backlogs per consumerSNS/EventBridge delivery to separate SQS queues
Durable progress across ordered stepsStep Functions workflow
EventBridge PutEvents example 
{
  "Entries": [{
    "Source": "com.example.orders",
    "DetailType": "OrderAccepted",
    "Detail": "{\"orderId\":\"o-42\",\"requestId\":\"r-42\"}",
    "EventBusName": "orders"
  }]
}

This illustrates the JSON PutEvents contract for a compatible configured bus. Check per-entry publication results and the exact bus mode; current EventBridge bus types have different feature contracts.

AWS reference: EventBridge capabilities · SNS fanout

AWS Step Functions

Coordinate application steps with explicit state and failure handling.

  • A state machine expresses service calls, branching and supported waits/retries/catches.
  • Lambda or ECS executes task code; Step Functions retains workflow progress. The workflow execution role needs target-service permissions.
  • Choose workflow type from duration, integration and execution-semantics requirements; make external side effects idempotent.

Decision boundary. CodePipeline coordinates software delivery; Step Functions coordinates application/business work. A workflow is optional when one handler or independent consumers suffice.

TypePrimary boundaryBilling shape
StandardDurable execution, up to one year; supported callback/job integrationsState transitions
ExpressShort high-volume execution, up to five minutes; integration differencesExecutions + duration/memory
Read the state type before choosing compute

Scroll the table horizontally on a narrow screen.

StateResponsibilityCaveat
TaskRun a supported service/API integration or activityA Lambda task runs code; workflow permission is still required
PassPass/transform state data without external workNot a substitute for arbitrary Lambda code
WaitPause until a time or for a durationWorkflow wait, not billable Lambda sleep
ChoiceEvaluate conditions and choose a next stateBranches do not themselves run a task
FailEnd execution with failure/error informationDoes not automatically undo already committed side effects

Exam trigger. Pause/branch explicitly across durable steps → state machine; use Task only where actual work is needed.

Amazon States Language: one application task 
{
  "StartAt": "RecordOrder",
  "States": {
    "RecordOrder": {
      "Type": "Task",
      "Resource": "arn:aws:states:::lambda:invoke",
      "Parameters": {"FunctionName": "orders", "Payload.$": "$"},
      "End": true
    }
  }
}

The sample omits retries and business error handling. Workflow execution semantics do not make an external payment exactly once; plan for uncertain task outcomes and replay.

AWS reference: Workflow types · Lambda integration · State types

AWS AppConfig

Validate and gradually deploy application configuration or feature flags.

  • Separate configuration data from the code artifact so supported behavior can change without rebuilding code.
  • Validators check configuration; deployment strategies control rollout. Configured monitoring can trigger recovery.
  • Applications retrieve configuration through supported agents/APIs. Parameter Store and Secrets Manager have different storage/rotation responsibilities.

Decision boundary. Creating a configuration version does not make every running process use it. Verify deployment, environment and application retrieval/cache behavior.

StartDeployment: illustrative identifiers 
{
  "ApplicationId": "a1b2c3d",
  "EnvironmentId": "e1f2g3h",
  "ConfigurationProfileId": "p1q2r3s",
  "ConfigurationVersion": "7",
  "DeploymentStrategyId": "d1e2f3g"
}

The application, environment, profile, validators, deployment strategy and monitoring must already be configured. Current pricing depends on retrieval/deployment usage; check AWS rates for the chosen retrieval pattern.

AWS reference: Configuration rollout · StartDeployment contract

AWS AppSync

Expose GraphQL APIs with real-time updates and supported offline-sync patterns.

  • Resolvers connect GraphQL fields to supported data sources such as DynamoDB or Lambda. Authorisation remains explicit.
  • GraphQL subscriptions deliver mutation-triggered real-time updates over managed connections. AppSync Events is a separate pub/sub API offering.
  • Offline synchronisation requires a client/local-store integration (for example Amplify DataStore) plus configured sync/versioned data sources; conflict detection/resolution is not automatic for every GraphQL API.

Decision boundary. Offline client state and server authorisation/conflict handling are separate responsibilities. A Cognito user pool authenticates users; an identity pool supplies scoped AWS credentials when needed.

NeedStarting featureCaveat
Live GraphQL updatesSubscriptionsSelection sets, auth and client connection matter
Offline edits + later syncCompatible client + AppSync sync/versioned sourceChoose optimistic concurrency, Automerge or Lambda conflict handling
JWT app sign-inCognito User PoolJWT is not an AWS access-key set
Direct AWS service accessCognito Identity Pool + roleTemporary AWS credentials; still constrained by IAM
Exam boundary: GraphQL sync vs identity

Exam trigger. Offline synchronisation and conflict handling → AppSync with the appropriate client/sync setup; Cognito alone does not sync application records.

Common trap. User pools issue app tokens; identity pools issue temporary AWS credentials. Neither is a substitute for resolver/data authorisation.

GraphQL subscription (schema excerpt) 
type Subscription {
  onUpdateOrder(id: ID!): Order
    @aws_subscribe(mutations: ["updateOrder"])
}
# Illustrative: define Order, Mutation, resolvers and auth separately.

Choose AppSync for the GraphQL and sync requirements, not because every API needs it.

AWS reference: Subscriptions · Sync and offline access · Conflict resolution

CloudFront & global delivery

Route and accelerate requests globally; run edge code only when a request needs custom processing.

  • CloudFront serves HTTP(S) through global Points of Presence (PoPs). An origin is a backend content source; path behaviours can select different origins.
  • Origin groups pair a primary with a secondary for configured failover. They do not combine responses.
  • Global Accelerator provides static anycast entry IPs and routes TCP/UDP traffic to healthy regional endpoints over the AWS backbone; it is not a content cache.

Decision boundary. Different paths → multiple origins. Same content with fallback → origin group. Custom edge logic → an edge function. Static global IPs → Global Accelerator.

CapabilityResponsibilityExample
CloudFront multiple originsRoute by cache behaviour/path pattern/images/* → S3; /api/* → ALB
Lambda@EdgeCustom request/response processingInspect request body or call another service at an eligible trigger
CloudFront origin groupRetry eligible requests against a secondaryPrimary 503 → backup origin
Global AcceleratorStatic anycast IPs, backbone routing and endpoint health/failoverClient → global entry IP → healthy regional ALB
Try it · CloudFront request router

Trace a cache miss: path routing and primary/secondary failover are separate choices.

Change the scenario

GET /images/logo.png → CloudFront PoP → S3. /api/orders routes to ALB. With a group, an eligible failed request retries a matching backup.

Assumes cache miss, allowed method and configured 503 failover; OPTIONS caching is enabled. Each path’s group has a backup serving the same content. No health probes or requests run here. Local learning model; no AWS requests.

Try it · CloudFront language cache key

Request English, then Japanese, before and after including lang in the cache key.

Change the example

Without lang in the key, /reviews?lang=en can populate /reviews, and a later lang=jp request hits the English response. Including lang separates variants.

One edge cache, unexpired entries, origin returns the requested language. In both modes the origin receives lang (via cache/origin-request policy); this isolates the cache-key mistake. Changing policy does not clear this local model’s previous entries. Local learning model; no AWS requests.

Routing, failover and edge code

Think of it as: A shopping-centre directory sends you to the right shop; a backup shop supplies the same item if the first fails. A worldwide phone number is a separate idea.

Flow. Viewer → CloudFront PoP → path behaviour → selected origin/group; optional edge code changes a request or response.

An origin group retries GET, HEAD or OPTIONS after a configured failure (for example 503); OPTIONS must be enabled as a cached method. It does not fail over POST/PUT, merge responses, or send all later requests directly to the backup. Each origin fetch tries the primary again.

An IPv4 Global Accelerator normally gets two static anycast IPv4 addresses (dual-stack also adds two IPv6 addresses). Anycast advertises the same address from multiple edge locations. That global public entry is separate from the regional ALB/NLB/EC2/Elastic IP endpoint.

Scroll the table horizontally on a narrow screen.

Edge codeRuns onGood fit / boundary
CloudFront FunctionsViewer request/response; JavaScriptShort header/URL/cache-key changes; no general network or request-body access
Lambda@EdgeViewer or origin request/response; supported Node.js/PythonMore processing, libraries, network or eligible request-body access; trigger restrictions apply

Exam trigger. A dynamic API alone needs no edge function. Choose code only when the scenario requires custom processing.

Common trap. Path routing, origin failover and global IP acceleration solve different problems.

Query strings: cache the representation, not just the path

Think of it as: Label each translated folder with its language; replacing wrongly labelled folders more often does not fix the labels.

  1. 1 · /reviews?lang=jp
  2. 2 · Cache key includes lang
  3. 3 · Separate Japanese response

A cache policy selects the request inputs in the cache key; query strings are not automatically included in every policy. If the origin varies /reviews by lang=en/jp/fr, include lang in the cache key. A header and a query parameter are distinct inputs.

The origin must receive the inputs it needs. Including a query parameter in the cache policy also forwards it; an origin-request policy can forward additional values without including them in the key. Forwarding lang while omitting it from the key can serve one cached language to everyone.

# Illustrative cache-policy fields
QueryStringsConfig:
  QueryStringBehavior: whitelist
  QueryStrings: [lang]
# /reviews?lang=en and /reviews?lang=jp now have different keys.

Exam trigger. Wrong cached variant despite correct origin response → inspect cache-key inputs before shortening TTL.

Common trap. A lower TTL reduces time until expiry, not the correctness of a key that collapses different representations.

Illustrative distribution rules (pseudocode) 
/images/* → images-origin (S3)
/api/*    → orders-origin (ALB)
# Either behaviour can instead target its own primary/secondary origin group.

Assume an origin fetch: a cache hit can be returned without contacting either origin. CloudFront can deliver dynamic responses without Lambda@Edge.

AWS reference: Origin failover · Edge function comparison · Global Accelerator · Cache policy inputs

AWS CodeCommit

Managed private Git repositories; repository encryption and Git authentication are separate responsibilities.

  • Repository data is encrypted at rest automatically with KMS; the default is the AWS-managed aws/codecommit key. HTTPS or SSH protects Git traffic in transit.
  • HTTPS can use IAM-generated CodeCommit Git credentials or the AWS credential helper. AWS access keys are not the direct Git username/password.
  • Git authenticates during clone, pull or push. A credential manager may supply stored credentials; Git has no standard git login command.

Decision boundary. GitHub PATs authenticate GitHub, not CodeCommit. Provider-managed at-rest encryption is not end-to-end encryption.

LayerMechanismResponsibility
At restDefault AWS-managed KMS key; supported customer-managed key optionCodeCommit encrypts automatically; ordinary use needs no separate encryption enablement
In transitHTTPS/TLS or SSHProtect the Git connection
HTTPS identityIAM-generated Git username/password, or AWS credential helperAuthenticate to CodeCommit; do not paste access keys as Git credentials
Credentials are a badge; encryption is the locked cabinet

Think of it as: The lock protects stored files; the badge proves who may open them. A GitHub badge does not open a CodeCommit door.

Flow. Local Git → HTTPS authentication → CodeCommit permissions → encrypted repository.

IAM-generated Git credentials are a service-specific username/password for an IAM user. The AWS CLI credential helper instead uses configured AWS credentials (including supported temporary credentials) to authenticate HTTPS requests. Configure the appropriate method rather than mixing conflicting helpers.

GitHub.com also encrypts repository data at rest and uses HTTPS/SSH in transit. In either service, the hosting provider can process repository contents; this is not client-only end-to-end encryption.

Exam trigger. HTTPS username/password for CodeCommit → IAM-generated Git credentials; federated AWS credentials → supported helper workflow.

Common trap. An AWS access key ID/secret is not the raw Git HTTPS username/password.

Executable migration pattern — use your own repositories 
git clone --mirror https://github.com/company/repo.git
cd repo.git
git push --mirror \
  https://git-codecommit.ap-southeast-2.amazonaws.com/v1/repos/my-repo
# Clone authenticates to GitHub if required; push authenticates to CodeCommit.
# --mirror copies refs and can delete destination refs: use a new migration target.

AWS reference: Encryption · HTTPS Git credentials · Credential helper · Current service availability
